Lecture 8: Splitting Components with ES Module Imports and Exports

Interview Question

CORE

How do you split components across files, and how do default and named imports differ?

Imagine this scenario:

  1. Julian opens the morning edition codebase for The National Times to add a breaking news banner.
  2. The editorial desk needs an article card and status badges shared across three different page layouts.
  3. A developer attempts to share the markup by copying and pasting the card function across multiple files.
  4. Why does every minor update to the card design trigger merge conflicts and duplicated bug fixes?
  5. Duplicated code drifts out of sync, displaying inconsistent article cards and broken badge colors in production.
  6. The team traps multiple components inside one giant file instead of organizing them into dedicated modules.
  7. Today, we organize components into clean modules, master default and named imports, and prevent silent import errors.

The Friction of Monolithic Files and Copy-Paste Components

Every web application grows from a single starter file into dozens of user interface sections. In static websites, developers often wrote all their markup inside one long document, copying chunks of HTML whenever they needed the same card on another page. In modern applications, keeping multiple components inside a single monolithic file makes code hard to read and impossible to share cleanly across pages. To solve this, JavaScript and React use modules: independent files that export components so other parts of your application can import and reuse them.

To see this in action on The National Times, you open your editor to build the article feed. At first, you write the ArticleCard component directly inside App.jsx. Then you write the Badge component in that same file. Before long, App.jsx stretches over twelve hundred lines of code. When another engineer wants to use ArticleCard on the search page, they cannot import it without importing the entire App component and all its unrelated layout logic.

It is possible that a developer may fall into the copy-paste trap when facing this limitation. They may copy the entire card function into the new search page file, thinking this avoids file refactoring. Now two identical copies of ArticleCard exist in the codebase. When a designer updates the card spacing or changes a CSS class, one copy gets updated while the other is forgotten. The two cards drift apart, creating visual bugs and confusing readers.

Consider a monolithic card component attempting to satisfy multiple editorial designs inside a single file:

Naive Monolithic Implementation
1function Badge({ text }) {
Trapped helper cannot be shared
2 return <span className="badge">{text}</span>;
3}
4function ArticleCard() {
Monolithic component definition
5 return (
6 <article className="card">
7 <Badge text="Latest News" />
8 </article>
9 );
10}

Notice what went wrong. The ArticleCard and Badge components are trapped inside the local scope of App.jsx. Other pages cannot reach them. If the editorial desk creates a new archive section, engineers must either duplicate the functions or cram the new section directly into App.jsx. As more features arrive, merge conflicts multiply, and finding a specific component becomes exhausting.

To resolve this architectural bottleneck, modern JavaScript and React rely on ES modules to organize components into dedicated files. You create a new file named ArticleCard.jsx under src/components/, export the card component, and import it wherever it is needed. Each component lives in its own file with its own clear responsibilities. When a design update occurs, you edit the component in one place, and every page that imports it automatically reflects the change.

⚡ IN THE WILD

Why do monolithic files create team friction?

Teams keeping multiple components inside one giant file suffer frequent git merge conflicts and code duplication. When two developers edit App.jsx simultaneously—one updating the article card while the other adjusts the primary layout—git reports a massive conflict because both touched the same giant file. If a developer copies the card to another page to bypass the file, bug fixes applied to one copy never reach the other. Organizing components into dedicated ES modules under src/components/ solves this by giving each component its own isolated file. Teams edit components independently, share them cleanly across pages, and eliminate duplicated code.

What Are ES Modules and How Does React Use Imports?

In modern web development, every JavaScript file is an isolated module. Variables, functions, and objects defined inside a module are private by default. Other files cannot access or modify them unless the file explicitly shares them using the export keyword. This isolation prevents global namespace collisions and keeps your codebase modular and predictable.

React components are standard JavaScript functions, so they use the official ECMAScript Module (ES Module) system built into the language. JavaScript provides two primary ways to export values from a module: default exports and named exports. A default export represents the primary value or component that a file provides, declared with export default A file can have at most one default export. In contrast, named exports allow a module to share multiple values or helper components, declared with export function Name()

When importing a named export, you place its exact name inside curly braces: import { Badge } from './ArticleCard.jsx' Notice the curly braces {}. In JavaScript, these braces look similar to object destructuring, but in module syntax they are a static language construct. They tell the JavaScript engine to link directly to the specific named export binding declared in that module. Unlike runtime object destructuring, ES module import bindings are evaluated and linked statically before any component function executes.

Under the hood, modern build tools like Vite use the ES module dependency tree to resolve files and package code for the browser. When you write an import statement, the bundler checks that the target file exists on disk and verifies that the requested export name matches an exported binding. If you import a named export with default syntax, or misspell the exported name, the build tool halts immediately with an explicit error before invalid code reaches the browser.

Principles of React: Splitting Components with Imports and Exports

When preparing for technical interviews, candidates must explain how components are organized across files, how default and named imports differ in mechanics and trade-offs, why exported functions must carry explicit names, and how the module dependency tree operates. To master these concepts, we formalize the six governing principles of component imports and exports:

PRINCIPLE 1

Give Each Shared Component Its Own Module

module boundary an isolated file that encapsulates internal logic and exposes explicit exports

Move a component into its own file under src/components/ when another file needs it or when its current file becomes hard to scan. Export the component from that file, and keep private helpers used by only one component unexported in that same file.

It is best practice to do this:
export default function ArticleCard() {
Dedicated module export
return <article className="card" />;
}
Instead of doing this:
function ArticleCard() {}
Monolithic file dumps everything
function Badge() {}
export default function App() {}

Moving a component into its own module takes three steps: (1) create a new file such as src/components/ArticleCard.jsx (2) export the component function from that file, and (3) import it in every file that renders it.

Top-level variables and helper functions defined in a module remain completely private unless you add the export keyword. If a helper function like formatDate is only used inside ArticleCard, keeping it unexported protects it from outside interference and keeps your module contract clean.

Private Module Encapsulation
1function formatDate(date) {
Private helper: NOT exported
2 return `Published on ${date}`;
3}
4export default function ArticleCard({ date }) {
5 return (
6 <article className="card">
7 <p>{formatDate(date)}</p>
8 </article>
9 );
10}

Notice what happens if another file attempts to import an unexported helper: import { formatDate } from './ArticleCard.jsx' The build immediately stops with an explicit error: [MISSING_EXPORT] "formatDate" is not exported by "src/components/ArticleCard.jsx" Unexported code remains strictly private to the module.

PRINCIPLE 2

Import Each Component in the Form It Was Exported

module linking the process where the JavaScript engine connects import statements to corresponding export declarations

Every file that renders a component must import it using the exact syntax matching its export. Use import Component from 'module-path' for a default export and import { Component } from 'module-path' for a named export. ES modules link imports to exports by kind and name before any component runs.

We should do this:
import ArticleCard from './ArticleCard.jsx';
Default import
import { Badge } from './ArticleCard.jsx';
Named import
We should not do this:
import { ArticleCard } from './ArticleCard.jsx';
Wrong: default
import Badge from './ArticleCard.jsx';
Wrong: named export

When you import a default export with curly braces (import { ArticleCard }), or import a named export without curly braces (import Badge), the syntax violates the module contract.

Watch how different tools report this error:

Build Error: Mismatched Default Import
1[MISSING_EXPORT] "ArticleCard" is not exported
Running vite build with a mismatched named import:
2 by "src/components/ArticleCard.jsx".
3file: /src/App.jsx:1:9
41: import { ArticleCard } from './components/ArticleCard.jsx';
5 ^

In Vite's development server, a mismatched default import blanks the page and displays an error in the browser console: "The requested module '/src/components/ArticleCard.jsx' does not provide an export named 'default'"

If you forget to write an import statement entirely, JavaScript throws a runtime error when executing the component: "ReferenceError: ArticleCard is not defined"

In legacy bundlers that used CommonJS module interop, importing a default export with braces evaluated to undefined. When React tried to render <ArticleCard />, it threw the famous error:

Legacy Bundler Runtime Error
1Element type is invalid: expected a string
Runtime crash on undefined
2(for built-in components) or a class/function
3(for composite components) but got: undefined.
4You likely forgot to export your component,
5or you mixed up default and named imports.

In modern native ES modules with Vite, the build tool stops the mistake earlier during module linking, protecting the browser from running broken code.

PRINCIPLE 3

Choose the Export Style by What the File Provides

name drift an inconsistency where different files import the same default export under different local names

Use a default export when a file exists to provide one primary component, and use named exports when a file provides multiple components or utilities. A default import can take any local variable name, while a named import must match the exported name character for character.

It is best practice to do this:
export default function ArticleCard() {}
Primary card export
export function Badge({ text }) {}
Secondary utility export
Instead of doing this:
import AuthorTag from './ArticleCard.jsx';
Silently renames card

The fundamental mechanical difference between default and named exports lies in name binding. Because a default export is the single fallback value of a module, the importing file can assign it any local variable name.

Look at how a default import permits arbitrary naming:

Arbitrary Default Import Naming
1import AuthorTag from './components/ArticleCard.jsx';
Misleading name
2
3export default function App() {
4 return (
5 <AuthorTag title="City News" />
Silently renders card
6 );
7}

The code above compiles and renders the article card with zero errors. However, it creates severe confusion: an engineer reading App.jsx thinks <AuthorTag /> is a small label, unaware that it renders an entire article card. Furthermore, searching the codebase for <ArticleCard /> will never find this usage.

In contrast, named exports strictly enforce that the import identifier inside curly braces matches the exported identifier. If you rename the named export Badge to StatusBadge in the source file, any file still importing { Badge } immediately fails to build with an explicit missing export error. Named exports make refactoring predictable and safe.

PRINCIPLE 4

Name Every Exported Component Function

anonymous component a component function declared without a name identifier in its definition

Always write exported components as named function declarations, such as export default function ArticleCard() {}. If you export an anonymous arrow function without a name, the JavaScript engine assigns it the fallback identifier default, and React prints <default> in its error callstacks and warnings.

We should do this:
export default function ArticleCard() {
Named function in error stacks
return <article>Latest News</article>;
}
We should not do this:
export default () => {
Anonymous export appears as <default>
return <article>Latest News</article>;
};

Official React documentation strongly discourages anonymous default exports like export default () => {} When a component function has no name, the JavaScript runtime assigns it the name of the export key, which is the literal string "default".

Look at what happens in the console when an anonymous component encounters a runtime error:

Error Stack: Anonymous Component Crash
1Uncaught Error: Failed to load article data
2 at default (ArticleCard.jsx:3:11)
Anonymous function lacks name
3The above error occurred in the <default> component:
4 at default (ArticleCard.jsx:2:1)
5 at App (App.jsx:5:3)

In a production codebase containing dozens of default-exported components, an error naming <default> provides zero clue about which component actually failed. You have to hunt through stack line numbers to find the file.

When you declare a named function, React displays the exact component name:

Error Stack: Named Component Crash
1Uncaught Error: Failed to load article data
2 at ArticleCard (ArticleCard.jsx:3:11)
Named function identified
3The above error occurred in the <ArticleCard> component:
4 at ArticleCard (ArticleCard.jsx:2:1)
5 at App (App.jsx:5:3)

Writing export default function ArticleCard() {} takes two seconds, guarantees clear React error stacks, and makes components easy to identify in React DevTools.

PRINCIPLE 5

Match Import Paths to Filenames Exactly, Including Case

case-sensitive file system an operating system storage model where uppercase and lowercase letters represent distinct files

Write every import path with the exact capitalization of the file on disk. The default macOS file system ignores letter casing and resolves ./components/articleCard.jsx to ArticleCard.jsx, while Linux build servers enforce strict case sensitivity and fail the build.

We should do this:
import ArticleCard from './components/ArticleCard.jsx';
Exact casing
We should not do this:
import ArticleCard from './components/articleCard.jsx';
Lowercase breaks

On macOS, the standard APFS file system is case-preserving but case-insensitive. If a file on disk is named ArticleCard.jsx, writing an import path with lowercase articleCard.jsx resolves and compiles with zero warnings on a developer's Mac laptop.

However, production build servers and continuous integration (CI) environments typically run Linux, where file systems are strictly case-sensitive. On Linux, articleCard.jsx and ArticleCard.jsx are completely different files. When your pull request runs in CI, the build crashes:

Linux CI Build Failure
1[UNRESOLVED_IMPORT] Could not resolve
Case mismatch fails Linux build
2 'components/articleCard.jsx' in src/App.jsx
3file: /home/runner/work/project/src/App.jsx:1:24
41: import ArticleCard from 'components/articleCard.jsx';
5 ^

This is one of the most frustrating "works on my machine" bugs in frontend engineering. Even worse, Git on macOS defaults to core.ignorecase = true. If you rename articleCard.jsx to ArticleCard.jsx in the Mac Finder, Git does not register the change. To fix the casing in Git, you must run an explicit rename command:

Terminal: Case-Sensitive Git Rename
1git mv src/components/articleCard.jsx \
2 src/components/ArticleCard.jsx
Forces Git to record casing

Always match the capitalization of your import paths to the exact filename on disk.

PRINCIPLE 6

Separate What Runs on Import from What Runs on Render

module evaluation the one-time execution of top-level code when a file is first imported
render execution the invocation of a component function by React to produce JSX markup

Importing a module executes its top-level code once when the module loads, regardless of how many files import it. In contrast, code placed inside a component function runs only when React actively renders that component in the user interface.

It is best practice to do this:
export default function ArticleCard() {
console.log("Render");
Runs on each component render
}
Instead of doing this:
console.log("Module");
Top-level code executes once on import
export default function ArticleCard() {}

In JavaScript, ES modules are singletons: when a file is imported for the first time, the JavaScript runtime evaluates all code written at the file's top level. If that same file is imported by five other components across your application, the top-level code does not execute again; the runtime returns the cached module export.

Look at how top-level module code compares to component render execution:

Module Evaluation vs Render Execution
1console.log('1. Module loaded');
Runs once on import
2
3export default function ArticleCard({ title }) {
4 console.log('2. Rendering component', title);
Runs on each render
5 return <article className="card">{title}</article>;
6}

Now observe what happens in the console when App.jsx imports ArticleCard and renders it twice:

Console Output on Application Startup
11. Module loaded: ArticleCard.jsx
Evaluated once on startup
22. Rendering component: Downtown Transit Accord Finalized
32. Rendering component: Historic Library Renovation Begins

Notice that "1. Module loaded: ArticleCard.jsx" prints exactly once when the file is imported. In contrast, "2. Rendering component:" prints twice because React rendered two card instances.

If App.jsx imports ArticleCard but never renders <ArticleCard /> on screen, the module still loads and prints "1. Module loaded", but the component function never executes. Bundlers include every imported module in the application package, so never put heavy calculations or unintended side effects at the module's top level.

Step 2
Next, we export the status badge as a named export
<ArticleCard.jsx>

We complete ArticleCard.jsx by rendering the card title and nested content, and then adding a secondary component: Badge. Some pages in our application only need to display a status badge without rendering a full article card. When designing a module that contains related sub-components, developers face an architectural crossroad:

  • Option 1 (The Single-Export File Shredding Way): Extract every single two-line helper into its own file (Badge.jsx, DateLabel.jsx), creating dozens of tiny files and cluttered import lists.
  • Option 2 (The Multi-Export Module Way): Keep the primary component as the default export and export closely related sub-components as named exports from the same file.

First, examine Option 1 with excessive file shredding:

Option 1: Over-Shredded Helper Files
1export default function Badge({ text }) {

2 return <span className="badge">{text}</span>;
3}

In Option 1, every tiny tag requires a separate file on disk, bloating your folder hierarchy and forcing parent components to manage numerous separate import statements.

In Option 2, ArticleCard.jsx exports its primary card as default and provides Badge as a named export from that same module:

10 <h2 className="card-title">{title}</h2>
11 <div className="card-body">{children}</div>
12 </article>
13 );
14}
15
16export function Badge({ text }) {
Secondary utility as named export
17 return <span className="status-badge">{text}</span>;
18}

Notice what Option 2 accomplishes. The primary job of ArticleCard.jsx is still the article card, so it remains the default export. But by exporting Badge with export function Badge the file allows other pages to import { Badge } directly without creating an artificial new file on disk.

Step 3
Finally, we import and compose the components inside
<App.jsx>

Now that src/components/ArticleCard.jsx provides both a default card and a named badge, we open src/App.jsx and import them. We use default import syntax for ArticleCard and named import syntax with curly braces for Badge. We render two distinct cards: one with a "LATEST NEWS" badge and another with an "ARCHIVE" badge. Notice that both files now have clear, focused jobs: ArticleCard.jsx manages card structure and badge styling, while App.jsx orchestrates page layout.

App.jsx

The single import statement import ArticleCard, { Badge } from './components/ArticleCard.jsx' imports both the default export and the named export in one concise line. The relative import path ./components/ArticleCard.jsx matches the on-disk file casing exactly, ensuring the project compiles cleanly on both macOS development laptops and Linux CI build servers.

Component Summary

App

The root application shell orchestrates the front-page feed layout. It imports the default article card and named badge helper from their dedicated component module. Notice it contains zero internal helper definitions or card markup of its own. Why? To maintain a clean, declarative container that composes modular components without file bloat.

ArticleCardtitle="..." date="..."

This is the primary article card component. It provides the default export for the module and encapsulates the card's internal layout and private helpers. Notice it exports the main card as a default export while exposing Badge as a secondary named export. When does this matter? To provide callers with a clear primary component while allowing flexible reuse of related sub-components.

In legacy web applications, keeping all components in a single monolithic file resulted in severe maintenance friction, frequent git merge conflicts, and copy-paste duplication. In React, splitting components into standard ES modules establishes clean architectural boundaries. ArticleCard.jsx acts as a dedicated module, exporting its primary component as a default export and secondary utilities as named exports. Because import syntax strictly dictates how values are consumed, developers enjoy build-time verification, clear stack traces, and seamless code reuse across the entire application.

Where you will meet this

  1. Design System Component Libraries: Enterprise UI libraries export primary components (like <Modal />) as default exports, while exposing sub-components (like { ModalHeader, ModalFooter }) as named exports.
  2. File-Based Routing Frameworks: Modern frameworks like Next.js and Remix require each page route file to export a single default React component to represent the page view.
  3. Utility and Icon Packages: Icon libraries package hundreds of SVG icons as individual named exports (import { SearchIcon, CloseIcon }), allowing bundlers to tree-shake unused icons from production bundles.

Glossary

  • Default Export: The primary value or component exported by a module, declared with export default and imported without curly braces under any local name.
  • Named Export: A specific value or component exported by a module using its declared name, imported inside curly braces matching the export identifier.
  • Module Dependency Tree: The hierarchical graph of file relationships formed by import and export statements, used by bundlers to package application code.
  • Render Tree: The runtime hierarchy of React component elements mounted on screen, evaluated by React during application rendering.
  • Name Drift: An inconsistency where different files import the same default export under different local names, making codebase searches difficult.

Beyond the basics

  • Official guide to importing and exporting components in React (see react.dev/learn/importing-and-exporting-components).
  • Official guide to understanding your UI as a tree, contrasting render trees with module dependency trees (see react.dev/learn/understanding-your-ui-as-a-tree#the-module-dependency-tree).
  • Code splitting and dynamic imports with React.lazy for on-demand bundle loading (see react.dev/reference/react/lazy).
  • Writing pure components that keep module scope free of unpredictable side effects (see react.dev/learn/keeping-components-pure).

Summary

➔ NEVER export anonymous component functions like export default () => {} because React prints <default> in error stacks and DevTools.

❒ Import Matching & Casing Discipline

➔ ALWAYS match import syntax to the export style, using default imports without braces for default exports and curly braces for named exports.

➔ ALWAYS write import paths with the exact casing of the filename on disk to prevent build failures on case-sensitive Linux CI servers.

Lecture 9: Mounting the Root Component with createRoot and Vite Tooling

Interview Question

CORE

How does your root component attach to the browser DOM with createRoot, and how do build tools assemble it?

Imagine this scenario:

  1. Elena starts her first morning at The National Times, tasked with launching the new digital newsroom prototype.
  2. She writes clean React components with JSX, expecting them to paint directly to the screen like standard HTML tags.
  3. She opens index.html in her web browser, but the screen stays entirely blank without rendering a single component.
  4. Why does a project filled with component code show nothing until an explicit mounting bridge attaches it to the page?
  5. Without a real DOM container and a running HTTP dev server, the browser halts with script errors or leaves an empty page.
  6. Developers often confuse core React component logic with the browser-specific renderer that mounts components to the DOM.
  7. Today, we master createRoot, connect virtual React elements to the real browser page, and understand how Vite serves our code.

The Mystery of the Empty Root Container

Every web application begins with an HTML document. When you build a website with traditional HTML, you write tags like <header>, <h1>, and <p> directly inside your files, and the browser parses and paints them immediately. In a React application, however, your components are JavaScript functions that return JSX markup. While you organize your components into modular files and export them cleanly, the browser cannot run JSX syntax on its own. It needs an explicit mounting bridge that connects your virtual component tree to a real, living HTML element on the page.

To see this in action on The National Times, imagine you are setting up the project for the morning edition. You write an App.jsx component that displays the newspaper title and an announcement banner. Then you open the project's root index.html file. Inside, you find almost nothing: just a standard HTML skeleton containing an empty <div id="root"></div> tag and a script tag. Looking at this empty container, a newcomer might wonder how component code ever makes its way onto the screen.

It is possible that a developer may fall into the naive script trap when trying to connect their code. They might try to link App.jsx directly inside index.html using a traditional <script src="/src/App.jsx"></script> tag, or double-click index.html to open it as a local file (file://) in Chrome. When they do, the browser fails immediately. The browser's native JavaScript parser encounters JSX tags like <App /> and halts with a fatal syntax error: Uncaught SyntaxError: Unexpected token '<'

Consider a naive attempt to load a React component directly through a classic HTML script tag:

Naive index.html Attempt
1<!DOCTYPE html>
2<html>
3 <head>
4 <script src="/src/App.jsx"></script>
Classic script cannot parse JSX tags
SyntaxError on JSX tags
5 </head>
6 <body><div id="root"></div></body>
7</html>

Notice what went wrong. The browser JavaScript engine only understands standard ECMAScript. When it hits JSX tags inside App.jsx, it halts because JSX is a syntax extension, not native browser JavaScript. Furthermore, opening index.html directly from your hard drive triggers security restrictions that prevent modern JavaScript modules from loading.

Years ago, older tutorials told developers to load monolithic React bundles through classic script tags and call ReactDOM.render(<App />, document.getElementById('root')) In React 19, that old method has been completely removed from the library. If you try to call ReactDOM.render today, JavaScript throws an error because the function no longer exists.

To display modern React components in the browser, applications rely on a clear mounting pipeline. First, index.html loads a JavaScript entry file, src/main.jsx, using a modern module script: <script type="module" src="/src/main.jsx"></script> Second, main.jsx imports createRoot from the browser renderer package, react-dom/client. Third, createRoot finds the physical HTML container on the page using document.getElementById('root') Finally, root.render(<App />) takes the virtual React element tree and mounts it directly into the real browser DOM. Meanwhile, a build tool like Vite transforms JSX on the fly and serves files over a local HTTP server so the browser can run them smoothly.

⚡ IN THE WILD

Why does double-clicking index.html fail to load React?

Developers opening index.html from their local desktop encounter a blank page and CORS errors in the browser console. When you double-click an HTML file, the browser loads it over the local file:// protocol. For security reasons, modern web browsers treat the local disk origin as null and block all ES module scripts (<script type="module">). The browser console logs: Access to script at 'file:///...' from origin 'null' has been blocked by CORS policy To run a modern React application, you must always serve your files over an HTTP server. During development, Vite provides an instant HTTP dev server (npm run dev), and for production builds, vite preview serves your compiled files locally over HTTP.

How React Connects to the Browser and Why Tools Transform Markup

To understand how React attaches to the screen, we must first recognize an important design decision: React separates the core component model from the browser renderer. The core package, named react, is responsible for creating elements, managing component logic, and calculating UI descriptions. It knows nothing about HTML tags or web browsers; in fact, the same core React library powers mobile applications in React Native. The browser renderer, named react-dom/client, is the bridge that turns those React element descriptions into real browser DOM elements like <div>, <article>, and <p>. In an application, only your entry file (main.jsx) imports from react-dom/client; all your component files import purely from react.

In standard JavaScript, document.getElementById('root') is a built-in browser DOM method. It searches the active HTML page for an element whose id attribute equals 'root'. If it finds the element, it returns a reference to that living DOM node in memory. If no element with that ID exists on the page, the method returns null. This DOM node is the physical home where React will place its elements.

In modern HTML, adding type="module" to a <script> tag tells the browser that the file uses modern JavaScript import and export statements. Unlike classic scripts, module scripts are automatically deferred by the browser. This means the browser downloads the script in the background while continuing to parse the HTML document. The script only executes after the entire HTML document has been parsed into memory. Because of this, a module script placed in the <head> of your page can safely find <div id="root"> even though the <div> is written further down in the <body>.

Browsers understand standard JavaScript, but they do not understand JSX tags like <h1> inside .jsx files. In addition, when you write import React from 'react' the browser does not know where to find node modules on your computer. This is why we use a build tool like Vite. During development, Vite runs a local HTTP server on http://localhost:5173. When the browser requests /src/main.jsx, Vite intercepts the request, transforms the JSX into standard JavaScript function calls in memory, and serves the result as native ES modules over HTTP. In production, vite build bundles all your code and styles into static files inside a dist/ directory that can be deployed to any web server.

Principles of React: Mounting the Root with createRoot

When preparing for technical interviews, candidates must clearly explain how React connects to the real browser DOM, why React 19 removed legacy mounting methods, how createRoot manages container contents and update timing, and how modern tooling like Vite powers development and production builds. To master these concepts, we formalize the eight governing principles of root mounting and tooling:

PRINCIPLE 1

Hand React One Container and Expect It to Replace That Container's Contents

container element a physical HTML tag on the page that React takes over to display its component tree
placeholder content temporary HTML placed inside the container that displays while JavaScript downloads

Give React ownership of one physical DOM element by passing it to createRoot. The first time you call root.render, React replaces all existing HTML inside that container with your component tree. Any HTML outside that container, such as a static header or footer in index.html, remains untouched in the browser.

It is best practice to do this:
<div id="root">
<p>Loading...</p>
React replaces container contents on mount
</div>
Instead of doing this:
<div id="root" />
<div id="extra-root" />
Avoid multiple mounting targets

When you call createRoot(container), you give React exclusive ownership of the DOM inside that specific element. When root.render(<App />) runs for the first time, React wipes whatever HTML was inside that container and replaces it with the rendered output of App.

This clearing behavior has a helpful practical benefit: you can place friendly placeholder HTML inside <div id="root">, such as <p>Loading The National Times...</p> While the user's browser downloads and parses the JavaScript bundles, this placeholder is visible on screen.

Container HTML with Loading Placeholder
1<header id="static-header">
Static masthead outside container remains untouched
2 <p className="site-title">The National Times</p>
3</header>
4
5<div id="root">
React takes over only what lives inside this container
6 <p className="loading">Loading newsroom feed...</p>
Cleared on mount
7</div>

As soon as React mounts, it replaces the loading paragraph with your actual newsroom application. Furthermore, any markup written outside the container, like the #static-header tag, stays completely intact in the Elements panel.

PRINCIPLE 2

Give createRoot an Element That Exists

null container error a fatal runtime crash thrown when createRoot receives null instead of a valid DOM element

Always pass createRoot a real, existing DOM node returned by document.getElementById. Make sure the identifier string matches the id in index.html character for character. Never pass createRoot a JSX element or a missing selector.

We should do this:
const element = document.getElementById('root');
Finds real DOM node
const root = createRoot(element);
Passes verified element
We should not do this:
const root = createRoot(document.getElementById('app'));
Typo is null
const root = createRoot(<App />);
Wrong: JSX is not a DOM node

createRoot expects exactly one parameter: a valid browser DOM element. If you make a typo in the identifier, such as typing document.getElementById('app') when index.html defines <div id="root">, the browser method finds nothing and returns null.

Passing null to createRoot causes React to throw a fatal error: "Target container is not a DOM element."

Target Container Validation
1const container = document.getElementById('root');
Real DOM element
2console.log(container);
Logs: <div id="root">
3
4const missing = document.getElementById('app');
Mistyped ID returns null
5console.log(missing);
Calling createRoot(null) throws fatal error:
Target container is not a DOM element.
Logs: null
6

The same error occurs if you mistakenly pass a JSX component directly into createRoot(<App />). In a modern Vite project, because the script uses type="module", the script is automatically deferred, so script position in HTML is not the cause. When you encounter this error, always verify that the container ID in index.html matches getElementById exactly.

PRINCIPLE 3

Render an Element with a Single Argument

React element a descriptor object created with JSX tags like <App /> that tells React what to mount

Call root.render with exactly one React element, such as <App />. Never pass the raw component function App without JSX tags, and never pass configuration options to render. Put root options directly inside createRoot(container, options).

We should do this:
const root = createRoot(container, options);
Root options go here
root.render(<App />);
Renders single React element with tags
We should not do this:
root.render(App);
Missing tags: passes function instead of element
root.render(<App />, options);
Invalid: render accepts 1 argument

Creating a root and rendering it are two distinct operations. Calling createRoot(container) prepares the container in memory, but nothing displays on screen until you call root.render().

When calling render, you must pass a React element (<App />), not a bare function (App). If you pass root.render(App), React logs a console error and leaves the page blank.

Passing Elements to root.render
1root.render(<App />);
Correct: pass a JSX element descriptor
Passes element descriptor
2
3root.render(App);
Wrong: passing the raw function
Missing JSX tags logs warning
4
5root.render(<App />, { prefix: 'news_' });
Wrong: passing options to render
Rejects extra arg

In addition, root.render accepts only one argument. If you need to configure root options, such as error logging handlers or identifier prefixes, pass them as the second argument to createRoot, not to render.

PRINCIPLE 4

Create the Root Once and Grow the App Inside App

single root architecture an application pattern where one root manages the entire component tree

Call createRoot exactly once at startup in main.jsx for your single page application. Add all new sections, feeds, and banners as components nested inside App, rather than creating multiple roots on the same container.

It is best practice to do this:
const root = createRoot(container);
One root at startup in main.jsx
root.render(<App />);
Instead of doing this:
createRoot(container).render(<NewsBanner />);
Duplicate root warns

In a project fully built with React, you should only call createRoot once in your entry file. If code in your application calls createRoot a second time on the same container, React detects the duplicate root and logs a clear warning.

Single Root vs Duplicate Root Warning
1const container = document.getElementById('root');
2const root = createRoot(container);
Single root initialization
3root.render(<App />);
4
5createRoot(container).render(<NewsBanner />);
Duplicate root call triggers warning:
Warning: Container already passed to createRoot()

Creating multiple roots on the same DOM element splits ownership, creates memory leaks, and breaks communication between components. If you want to add new user interface elements, like a breaking news banner or a sidebar, add them as child components inside App.jsx. In standard React development, components update by changing their state, not by calling root.render repeatedly.

PRINCIPLE 5

Serve the App Over HTTP Through Vite

HTTP protocol the web communication protocol that allows browsers to load modules and fetch assets safely
file protocol the local disk protocol that browsers restrict from executing modern module scripts

Run the Vite development server using npm run dev during development, and serve the built dist/ directory from a web server using vite preview. Never double-click index.html from your desktop or load files over the file:// protocol.

It is best practice to do this:
$ npm run dev
Serves native ES modules over HTTP
Instead of doing this:
$ open ~file:
index.html~ // Local file protocol blocks ES modules

Modern web browsers enforce strict security rules around ES modules. When you open an HTML file from your hard drive using the file:// protocol, the browser treats the origin as null. When index.html tries to load <script type="module" src="/src/main.jsx"> Chrome blocks the script with a CORS security error.

Vite HTTP Development Server
1$ npm run dev
Starting Vite development server
2
3 VITE v6.0.0 ready in 180 ms
4
5 ➜ Local: http://localhost:5173/
Serves modules over HTTP
6 ➜ Network: use --host to expose

The same failure happens if you double-click dist/index.html after running vite build, because the production HTML requests /assets/index-[hash].js from the server root. To run a modern React application, you must serve it over HTTP. Vite provides npm run dev for instant development with hot module replacement, and vite preview to test your production build on a local HTTP server.

PRINCIPLE 6

Keep JSX in .jsx Files

JSX file extension the explicit file suffix that tells build tools to compile JSX markup into function calls

Name every file that contains JSX syntax with the .jsx extension, such as App.jsx or main.jsx. Vite transforms JSX only in .jsx and .tsx files, and treats standard .js files as plain JavaScript.

It is best practice to do this:
export default function App() { return <h1>News</h1>; }
File: ~App.jsx~
Compiles JSX
Instead of doing this:
export default function App() { return <h1>News</h1>; }
File: ~App.js~
Fails in Vite

In older build setups like Create React App, developers often placed JSX markup inside files ending in .js. Vite adopts a faster, stricter architecture: it parses files ending in .js as standard ECMAScript.

If you leave JSX tags inside a file named App.js, Vite's transformer stops with an explicit build error:

Vite Transform Build Error
1[builtin:vite-transform] Unexpected JSX expression
Fails in plain .js
2file: /Users/developer/project/src/App.js:2:11
31: export default function App() {
42: return <h1>The National Times</h1>;
5 ^

The error message does not explicitly mention the file extension, which can confuse developers who are used to older tools. By naming every file containing JSX with .jsx, you ensure Vite applies its fast React compiler plugin and converts your tags into valid JavaScript.

PRINCIPLE 7

Mount with createRoot from react-dom/client

client entry point the react-dom/client subpath providing root creation methods for web browsers

Import createRoot directly from react-dom/client in your entry file. Never import render from react-dom, because React 19 completely removed the legacy ReactDOM.render and ReactDOM.hydrate methods.

We should do this:
import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
Modern mounting API
const root = createRoot(document.getElementById('root'));
We should not do this:
import { render } from 'react-dom';
Removed in React 19: undefined
render(<App />, document.getElementById('root'));
Crashes runtime

Developers returning to React after several years often reach for import { render } from 'react-dom' In React 19, the legacy render, hydrate, and unmountComponentAtNode functions were removed entirely.

If you attempt to import render from 'react-dom', the imported value is undefined. Calling render(...) immediately crashes in the browser:

React 19 Mounting Bridge
1import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';
Client renderer
2import App from './App.jsx';
3
4const container = document.getElementById('root');
5const root = createRoot(container);
Creates concurrent root
6root.render(<App />);
Legacy render removed in React 19:
Import { render } from 'react-dom' -> TypeError
7

The modern mounting API lives exclusively in 'react-dom/client'. Furthermore, keeping createRoot isolated in main.jsx ensures that your component files (App.jsx, NewsBanner.jsx) remain pure: they import only from 'react', keeping them independent of browser-specific mounting code.

PRINCIPLE 8

Expect root.render to Update the DOM After Your Code Continues

scheduled rendering the asynchronous process where React queues updates and paints the DOM after current code finishes

Understand that root.render schedules the rendering work asynchronously rather than updating the browser DOM immediately on the same line. Code written immediately after root.render still sees the container's old HTML content.

It is best practice to do this:
root.render(<App />);
Schedules async render queue
Instead of doing this:
root.render(<App />);
console.log(container.innerHTML);
Stale: DOM has not updated yet

When developers come to React from imperative JavaScript, they often expect functions to complete all their work immediately. If you write root.render(<h1>The National Times</h1>) and on the very next line write console.log(document.getElementById('root').innerHTML) the console does not log your new heading! Instead, it logs the old placeholder text that was originally inside <div id="root">.

Asynchronous Render Execution
1const container = document.getElementById('root');
2const root = createRoot(container);
3
4root.render(<h1>The National Times</h1>);
Schedules async render
5
6console.log(container.innerHTML);
Next line executes before React paints DOM:
Logs stale placeholder markup

This happens because root.render does not block the main browser thread to mutate the DOM synchronously. It schedules a render task in React's internal queue. React evaluates your components, calculates the differences, and paints the real browser DOM only after your current JavaScript execution frame finishes and yields back to the browser.

Step 1
First, we inspect the host HTML document
<index.html>

We start at the root of the project by inspecting index.html. Unlike traditional web pages that contain hundreds of lines of static content, our React host document contains a clean, minimal shell. Inside the <body>, we define <div id="root"> with a loading placeholder that appears while JavaScript loads. Crucially, we link our entry point using <script type="module" src="/src/main.jsx"></script> Because this script tag has type="module", the browser defers execution until the HTML document is fully parsed, ensuring document.getElementById('root') can always find the container.

index.html
1<!DOCTYPE html>
2<html lang="en">
3 <head>
4 <title>The National Times</title>
5 </head>
6 <body>
7 <div id="root"><p>Loading...</p></div>

8 <script type="module" src="/src/main.jsx"></script>
Entry script
9 </body>
10</html>

Notice the structure of index.html. The <div id="root"> element acts as the single boundary that React will control. The <script type="module"> tag tells the browser to treat main.jsx as an ES module and load it after the document is parsed.

Step 2
Next, we construct the root component
<src/App.jsx>

With our host HTML defined, we create src/App.jsx. This component acts as the root of our React component tree. Notice that App.jsx imports purely from 'react' and child component files; it contains zero imports from 'react-dom' or 'react-dom/client'. By keeping App isolated from the DOM mounting bridge, our component remains pure, testable, and reusable. In this step, App renders the newsroom header and prepares a container for our child news banner.

App.jsx
1import NewsBanner from './components/NewsBanner.jsx';

2
3export default function App() {

10}

Notice how App acts as the orchestrator. It imports NewsBanner as a child component and passes it a message prop. It never tries to interact with document.getElementById or manipulate browser DOM nodes directly.

Step 3
Then, we declare the child banner component
<src/components/NewsBanner.jsx>

Following our single-root rule, we grow our application by adding components inside App, rather than creating new roots. We create src/components/NewsBanner.jsx to display editorial announcements. It receives a message prop, displays a "LATEST NEWS" badge, and wraps the text in a clean container. Because this component lives in its own module, the editorial desk can update its layout without touching either App.jsx or the mounting entry file.

NewsBanner.jsx

Step 4
Finally, we initialize createRoot and mount the tree
<src/main.jsx>

Finally, we connect our React application to the browser page in src/main.jsx. We import createRoot from 'react-dom/client', and import our top-level App component. We find the container element using document.getElementById('root') We check that the element exists, pass it to createRoot, and call root.render(<App />) with our root JSX tag. When Vite serves this project, React mounts App, clears the loading placeholder, and renders our complete newsroom interface into the browser window.

main.jsx
1import { createRoot } from 'react-dom/client';

2import App from './App.jsx';
3

5

9}

Notice the clean sequence in main.jsx. We first find the container node. We verify it exists with if (container) before passing it to createRoot. Once the root is initialized, root.render(<App />) mounts the virtual tree into the physical container.

Component Summary

App

The root application component serves as the top-level parent for all newsroom UI. It composes layout elements and child components like NewsBanner. Notice it imports only from React and child modules, remaining completely independent of browser DOM mounting code.

main

The application entry point bridges React to the browser DOM. It imports createRoot from react-dom/client, finds the container element, and mounts <App /> using root.render. When does this execute? It runs once at startup when the browser loads the module script.

NewsBannermessage="..."

The leaf announcement component displays breaking news alerts inside the feed. It receives text data through props and encapsulates banner styling. Why does it live inside App? Because all new UI grows inside the single root component tree rather than creating extra roots.

In modern web applications, mounting a React application to the browser is a clear, deliberate process. The browser loads index.html, which provides an empty container and requests main.jsx as an ES module. In main.jsx, createRoot takes exclusive ownership of that container and mounts the <App /> component tree with root.render. Vite powers the entire development workflow by compiling JSX on demand and serving files over HTTP. By separating the core React component model from the ReactDOM mounting bridge, React ensures your components stay clean, modular, and ready to render anywhere.

Where you will meet this

  1. Project Scaffolding and Setup: When you create a new application using Vite (npm create vite@latest), the generator creates index.html, src/main.jsx, and src/App.jsx using this exact createRoot mounting architecture.
  2. Embedding React in Existing Web Pages: When adding React to an existing server-rendered website (such as WordPress, Django, or Rails), you identify a single <div> on the page and mount a standalone React widget into it with createRoot.
  3. Application Diagnostic Audits: During production debugging, senior engineers inspect main.jsx to verify that root configuration options, error logging handlers, and StrictMode boundaries are correctly configured.

Glossary

  • createRoot: The modern React DOM client method that creates a concurrent root container for a physical browser element.
  • root.render: The root method that schedules the rendering of a React element tree into the designated DOM container.
  • DOM Container: The physical HTML element, typically <div id="root">, that React takes over to manage its user interface.
  • Module Script: An HTML <script type="module"> tag that loads ES modules and automatically defers execution until HTML parsing completes.
  • Vite Dev Server: A local development server that compiles JSX on demand and serves native ES modules over HTTP with instant updates.
  • Single Root Architecture: An application design pattern where one root manages the entire user interface tree from a single top-level component.

Beyond the basics

  • Official reference documentation for createRoot and its configuration options (see react.dev/reference/react-dom/client/createRoot).
  • Official guide to building a modern React application from scratch with tools like Vite (see react.dev/learn/build-a-react-app-from-scratch).
  • Official guide to adding React to an existing project or multi-page website (see react.dev/learn/add-react-to-an-existing-project).
  • React 19 upgrade guide detailing the removal of ReactDOM.render and legacy mounting methods (see react.dev/blog/2024/04/25/react-19-upgrade-guide).

Lecture 10: Conditional Rendering in React

Interview Question

CORE

How do you show, hide, or switch JSX based on a condition?

Imagine this scenario:

  1. Elena sits down at her desk at The National Times to build the morning edition article header.
  2. She needs to display a red "BREAKING NEWS" alert for urgent events, show a live coverage badge for ongoing stories, and hide comments when disabled.
  3. She adds an unread comment indicator with {commentCount && <Comments />} and runs the code, but an ugly stray 0 appears right across the header.
  4. Why does JavaScript print a raw number 0 onto the page when you expect nothing to render?
  5. Relying on imperative DOM class toggles (el.classList.add('hidden')) causes layout flickering and fights React's rendering pipeline.
  6. Many developers struggle to choose between early returns, ternaries, and logical AND operators when branching their markup.
  7. Today, we master declarative conditional rendering in React, understand falsy evaluation, and build clean, reliable UI branches.

The Friction of Imperative DOM Branching

Every web interface exists to adapt to dynamic conditions (such as displaying breaking news alerts, showing live updates, or toggling reader comments). In static HTML documents, all elements are hardcoded as permanent text, while in modern applications that data changes constantly based on incoming server responses. To reflect these changes on screen, traditional web scripts searched the browser document and manually toggled CSS classes or modified element styles step by step.

To see this in action on The National Times, you open your editor to build the article header component: ArticleHeader.jsx. You need to display a red "BREAKING NEWS" badge when an article is marked as urgent, show a pulsating "LIVE" badge during ongoing coverage, and hide the reader comments section whenever comments are disabled for a story.

It is possible that a developer coming from vanilla JavaScript may attempt to handle these variations by searching the DOM and toggling CSS classes directly. They might render all possible badges into the HTML, and then write helper functions that query the DOM to hide elements:

Naive DOM Mutation Attempt
1function updateArticleVisibility(isBreaking) {
2 const badge = document.querySelector('.breaking-badge');
Manual DOM query
3 if (!isBreaking && badge) {
4 badge.classList.add('hidden');
Fights React DOM reconciliation
5 }
6}

Notice what went wrong. The helper function searches the real browser document using document.querySelector and modifies class lists behind React's back. Because React maintains its own virtual description of the user interface in memory, manual DOM mutations quickly fall out of sync with the component tree. When a parent re-renders, React reconciles the tree and overwrites the manual changes, causing visual flickering and hard-to-track layout bugs. Furthermore, elements hidden with display: none remain physically present in the DOM tree and the accessibility tree, wasting browser memory and confusing assistive technologies like screen readers.

In legacy web development, developers regularly kept invisible elements in the DOM and toggled their visibility using jQuery scripts like $('#badge').hide(). In a modern declarative framework like React, this approach violates the fundamental principle that user interface is a pure projection of data (UI = f(data)).

To solve this problem, React introduces declarative conditional rendering. Instead of creating elements and then hiding them by mutating the DOM, you decide which elements exist in the first place directly inside your component function. React does not invent a special templating syntax or custom attributes like v-if or ngIf. Instead, you use standard JavaScript control flow: if statements for early returns, the ternary operator (? :) for choosing between two alternate elements, and the logical AND operator (&&) for including an element or rendering nothing. When a condition evaluates to false, React leaves that element out of the virtual tree entirely, meaning it is never created in the browser DOM.

⚡ IN THE WILD

Why does a stray 0 print on the screen when using logical AND?

Developers writing {commentCount && <Comments />} discover a literal number 0 rendered on the screen when an article has zero comments. In JavaScript, 0 && <Component /> evaluates to the number 0, not false. The logical AND operator evaluates the left side first; because 0 is falsy, JavaScript short-circuits and returns that exact value (0). When React receives 0 inside curly braces, it does not hide it. React suppresses booleans (false), null, and undefined, but it always treats numbers as visible user content. As a result, React creates a real browser text node containing "0" and paints it directly onto the screen. To prevent this bug, you must always convert numeric checks to explicit boolean comparisons, such as {commentCount > 0 && <Comments />}

How React Evaluates Conditions and Suppresses Falsy Values

To master conditional rendering in React, we must first understand how React evaluates your code. In many other frameworks, conditional rendering relies on proprietary template directives that you write as custom HTML attributes. In React, components are standard JavaScript functions. Because JSX compiles directly into JavaScript function calls (_jsx(...)), you have the full power of JavaScript at your disposal. You can use standard if statements, store JSX elements in local variables, evaluate ternary expressions, and short-circuit with logical operators. You do not need to learn a separate templating language.

In earlier lessons, you learned that curly braces {} inside JSX open an evaluation window where you can write JavaScript. However, JavaScript distinguishes between statements and expressions. An expression is a unit of code that evaluates to a single value, such as 2 + 2, article.title, or a function call. A statement is an instruction that controls program execution, such as if (condition) { ... }, for, or while. Function arguments and object properties can only accept expressions. Because JSX compiles into function calls, you cannot place an if statement directly inside JSX curly braces (<div>{if (isLive) { ... }}</div> throws a fatal syntax error). For inline branching inside markup, you must use expressions like the ternary operator or logical AND.

For developers who are newer to JavaScript, let us briefly review the ternary operator (? :). The ternary operator is a compact, inline conditional expression that takes three parts: a condition, followed by a question mark (?), an expression to execute if the condition is truthy, followed by a colon (:), and an expression to execute if the condition is falsy. For example, isLive ? <LiveBadge /> : <StaticDate /> checks the isLive variable. If isLive is true, the expression evaluates to <LiveBadge />. If isLive is false, it evaluates to <StaticDate />. Because the entire ternary evaluates to a single concrete value, it fits cleanly inside JSX curly braces.

Similarly, let us review the logical AND operator (&&). In JavaScript, the && operator evaluates expressions from left to right using short-circuit evaluation. If the left operand is truthy, JavaScript evaluates and returns the right operand. If the left operand is falsy, JavaScript stops immediately and returns the value of that left operand without evaluating the right side. For example, in isBreaking && <span className="alert">BREAKING</span> if isBreaking is true, JavaScript evaluates the right side and returns the JSX element. If isBreaking is false, JavaScript stops and returns false.

Now comes the crucial link between JavaScript evaluation and React rendering: the suppression whitelist. When React encounters a value inside JSX curly braces, it inspects that value before touching the browser DOM. If the value is false, null, undefined, or true, React considers it an empty slot and renders zero DOM nodes. It produces no HTML tags, no text, and no whitespace. However, if the value is a string or a primitive number, React does not suppress it. React treats strings and numbers as legitimate user content and renders them as real browser text nodes. This is why returning null from a component renders nothing, why false && <Badge /> renders nothing, and why 0 && <Badge /> renders a visible "0".

Principles of React: The Core Laws of Conditional Rendering

When preparing for technical interviews, candidates must clearly explain how to show, hide, and branch markup using standard JavaScript, why numeric values cause the classic stray zero bug, how early returns protect components against missing data crashes, and when to extract complex conditions into plain JavaScript variables. To master these concepts, we formalize the five governing principles of conditional rendering:

PRINCIPLE 1

Return Early When the Component Cannot Produce Its Output

early return exiting a component function early with null or fallback markup before reaching the main return
defensive guarding checking that data exists before reading its nested properties

When a component depends on data to display its content, check for that data at the top of the function. Return null or a fallback before reading any properties so missing data does not crash your render. If the parent component decides whether the element belongs on screen at all, place the condition directly in the parent's JSX.

It is best practice to do this:
function ArticleHeader({ article }) {
if (!article) return null;
Returns early before reading missing data
return <h1>{article.title}</h1>;
}
Instead of doing this:
function ArticleHeader({ article }) {
return <h1>{article.title}</h1>;
Crashes if article is undefined
}

When a component receives its data as a prop, there are times when that data has not yet arrived or is completely undefined. If you attempt to access nested properties on missing data, such as writing <h1>{article.title}</h1> when article is undefined, the JavaScript runtime throws a fatal error: Uncaught TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'title')

This halts the entire rendering process and unmounts the user interface. By placing an early return at the very top of your component (if (!article) return null;), you intercept the missing state before any property access occurs.

Child Early Return Guard
1function ArticleHeader({ article }) {
Input prop
2 if (!article) {
3 return null;
Prevents crash on article.title
4 }
5 return <h1>{article.title}</h1>;
6}
Parent Inclusion Guard
1function Feed({ currentArticle }) {
2 return (
3 <main>
4 {currentArticle && (
Parent decides child presence
5 <ArticleHeader article={currentArticle} />
6 )}
7 </main>
8 );
9}

When a component returns null, React paints nothing for that component in the DOM, leaving an empty slot while preserving the rest of the page. If the component should display a temporary loading state instead of an empty space, you can return a fallback element such as <p>Loading article...</p> However, returning null from deep within a child component can sometimes surprise a teammate reading the parent code; whenever the decision is purely whether the parent should render the child, it is cleaner to write the guard in the parent's own JSX ({article && <ArticleHeader article={article} />}).

PRINCIPLE 2

Use && for Show-or-Nothing and the Ternary for One of Two

logical AND operator a JavaScript operator (&&) that renders the right-hand element only when the left condition is true
ternary operator a JavaScript inline conditional operator (? :) that chooses between two alternative values

Use the logical AND operator (&&) when you want to show an element or render nothing at all. Use the ternary operator (? :) when you need to choose between two different elements. Matching the operator to the shape of your condition keeps both outcomes clear and prevents duplicated logic.

It is best practice to do this:
{isLive ? <LiveBadge /> : <StaticDate />}
Single ternary for 2 choices
Instead of doing this:
{isLive && <LiveBadge />}
{!isLive && <StaticDate />}
Duplicating inverse conditions

In technical interviews, interviewers frequently evaluate whether a developer understands the distinct architectural roles of the logical AND operator (&&) and the ternary operator (? :). A common mistake is using two separate && expressions with opposite conditions to simulate an if/else branch: {isLive && <LiveBadge />} followed by {!isLive && <StaticDate />}

This pattern is fragile because it duplicates the condition in two places. If another engineer later updates the condition for the live badge but forgets to update the inverted condition below it, both elements or neither element may render at the same time.

Operator Selection by Branch Shape
1{isBreaking && <span className="alert">BREAKING</span>}
SHOW-OR-NOTHING: renders badge when true, nothing when false
2
3{isLive ? <LiveBadge /> : <StaticDate />}
CHOICE BETWEEN TWO: picks one of two alternative elements

When your user interface requires choosing between two alternate elements (Branch A or Branch B), the ternary operator expresses this intent in a single, unified expression. Conversely, when your interface requires showing an element or nothing at all (Branch A or Nothing), writing {isBreaking ? <span className="alert">BREAKING</span> : null} is needlessly verbose. The logical AND operator ({isBreaking && <span className="alert">BREAKING</span>}) cleanly expresses show-or-nothing, relying on React's suppression whitelist to discard the false result when the condition is not met.

PRINCIPLE 3

Make the Left Side of && an Explicit Boolean

stray zero an unwanted 0 displayed on screen when a numeric zero short-circuits in JSX
explicit boolean comparison using a comparison operator like count > 0 to produce a real true or false value

Always convert numbers and arrays to a real boolean before using the && operator in JSX. JavaScript returns the value of the left side whenever it is falsy, and React renders numbers directly to the screen. Comparing a number with zero (count > 0) produces true or false, preventing an unwanted 0 or NaN from appearing on your page.

It is best practice to do this:
{commentCount > 0 && <span>Comments</span>}
Explicit boolean check
Instead of doing this:
{commentCount && <span>Comments</span>}
Raw zero prints on screen

The most infamous trap in React conditional rendering is the stray zero bug. A developer may assume that because 0 is a falsy value in JavaScript, writing {commentCount && <Comments />} will render nothing when commentCount equals 0.

Look at what JavaScript physically executes: when evaluating 0 && <Comments />, JavaScript checks the left operand. Because 0 is falsy, the && operator short-circuits and evaluates to the number 0. It does NOT evaluate to false. React then receives 0 inside the curly braces.

Raw Number Zero Trap
1const commentCount = 0;
Raw numeric zero value
2<div>{commentCount && <span>Comments</span>}</div>
Paints stray 0
Safe Boolean Comparisons
1<div>{commentCount > 0 && <span>Comments</span>}</div>
Comparison produces boolean false: React renders nothing
2
3<div>{tags.length > 0 && <TagList tags={tags} />}</div>
Length check avoids rendering empty container markup

According to React's suppression whitelist, false, null, and undefined are ignored, but numbers are always preserved as valid content. Therefore, React creates a living browser DOM text node containing "0" and paints it directly onto the screen. The exact same trap occurs with NaN: if an uninitialized calculation results in NaN, writing {rating && <StarRating />} causes React to render the string "NaN" on screen while logging a console warning: "Received NaN for the children attribute. If this is expected, cast the value to a string." Similarly, passing an empty array tags = [] directly to {tags && <TagList />} renders an empty list because empty arrays are truthy in JavaScript. To guarantee your conditions behave predictably, never rely on raw numeric truthiness on the left of &&; always convert the condition into an explicit boolean comparison: write commentCount > 0 && ..., !Number.isNaN(rating) && ..., or tags.length > 0 && ....

PRINCIPLE 4

Move Branching Out of JSX When It Outgrows One Expression

nested ternary chaining multiple ? : operators inside one expression, making code difficult to read
variable extraction calculating markup in JavaScript variables before returning the main JSX tree

When conditional logic grows beyond a single inline choice, move the calculation out of JSX into standard if statements with a variable or a lookup table before the return. Keeping complex branching in plain JavaScript avoids confusing nested ternaries and makes your code easy to read, test, and update.

It is best practice to do this:
let badge = null;
if (isBreaking) badge = <span className="alert">BREAKING</span>;
else if (isLive) badge = <span className="live">LIVE</span>;
return <header>{badge}<h1>{title}</h1></header>;
Flat, readable JSX
Instead of doing this:
return (
<header>
{isBreaking ? <Alert /> : isLive ? <Live /> : null}
Nested ternary
<h1>{title}</h1>
</header>
);

When building real-world user interfaces, a component often needs to choose between three or more visual states. For example, an article badge area might need to display a red "BREAKING" badge for urgent alerts, a blue "LIVE" badge for ongoing coverage, a grey "ARCHIVED" tag for older dispatches, or nothing at all for standard stories.

When developers try to force all this logic inline inside JSX curly braces, they end up writing nested ternary expressions: {isBreaking ? <Alert /> : isLive ? <Live /> : isArchived ? <Archive /> : null} Teammates struggle to parse this code. Finding which colon corresponds to which question mark requires mental gymnastics, and adding a new case requires editing a fragile inline chain.

Extracted Variable Branching
1let badge = null;
Default empty slot
2if (status === 'breaking') {
3 badge = <span className="badge alert">BREAKING</span>;
4} else if (status === 'live') {
5 badge = <span className="badge live">LIVE</span>;
6}
7return <header>{badge}<h1>{title}</h1></header>;
Embeds precomputed JSX

In React, JSX is just JavaScript. You are not forced to write everything inside the return statement. When conditional branching outgrows a single clean expression, extract the logic before the return statement using standard let variables and if/else statements, or a clean lookup table. You assign the resulting JSX element (or null) to a variable such as let statusBadge = null; and then embed {statusBadge} cleanly inside your returned markup. This keeps your JSX clean, readable, and easy to maintain.

PRINCIPLE 5

Omit Elements Through JSX Instead of Hiding Them with DOM Commands

DOM omission completely leaving an element out of the rendered DOM tree using a JSX condition
imperative class toggle manually adding or removing CSS classes like hidden using document queries

Control whether an element exists on the page by including or omitting it in JSX, rather than searching the page and modifying CSS classes by hand. When JSX omits an element, React leaves it out of the DOM entirely. If an element must remain in the DOM while hidden, pass a CSS class or the hidden prop through JSX.

It is best practice to do this:
{showComments && <section>Comments</section>}
Omitted from real DOM
Instead of doing this:
el.classList.add('hidden');
Mutates classes behind React

In declarative web engineering, there is a fundamental architectural difference between omitting an element and hiding an element. When you conditionally render an element using JSX ({showComments && <Comments />}), React physically includes or excludes the element from the rendered DOM. When showComments is false, the <section className="comments"> element does not exist in the browser DOM at all.

If you run document.querySelector('.comments') in the browser console, it returns null. It consumes zero memory and is completely absent from the browser accessibility tree.

Declarative Visibility Control
1{showComments && <section className="comments">Discussion</section>}
DOM OMISSION: element is absent from DOM; query returns null
2
3<section className="comments" hidden={!showComments}>
DECLARATIVE CSS HIDING: node stays in DOM but hidden from view
4 Discussion
5</section>

In contrast, if you render the element and hide it with CSS (display: none or <section className="comments" hidden>), the DOM node still physically exists in browser memory. It continues to occupy space in the document object model, can still be found by DOM queries, and may retain focus or form state. Never attempt to manipulate classes on React-managed nodes using imperative scripts like classList.add('hidden'), because manual mutations fight React's reconciliation engine. If an element should not be part of the UI, omit it through JSX. If the physical node must stay in the DOM while hidden, control its visibility declaratively by passing a class or the hidden boolean prop through JSX: <section hidden={!showComments}>

<src/components/ArticleHeader.jsx>

Second, it extracts reading time logic before the return statement using a clean if statement and a let readingBadge variable, avoiding nested ternaries. Third, inside the JSX markup, it uses logical AND with an explicit boolean check (isBreaking && ...) to display a red "BREAKING NEWS" alert. Fourth, it uses a ternary operator (isLive ? <LiveBadge /> : <span className="date">{date}</span>) to choose between live coverage and a static timestamp. Component Summary

App

The root application shell manages layout and feeds data into the component tree. It defines sample article fixtures with varied flags (breaking, live, comment counts) and passes them to child components through props.

ArticleHeaderarticle={...}

The conditional header boundary handles all branching logic. It executes an early return for missing data, pre-calculates topic badges before return, and uses ternaries and boolean-guarded logical AND operators inside JSX.

LiveBadge

The leaf live indicator encapsulates the visual markup and pulsing animation for live news coverage. It is conditionally mounted by ArticleHeader only when the article's isLive flag evaluates to true.

Declarative conditional rendering fundamentally changes how developers build dynamic interfaces. Instead of mutating the DOM after elements are created, React components describe exactly which elements should exist for any given combination of props. By using early returns for missing data, ternaries for binary choices, boolean-guarded logical AND operators for show-or-nothing branches, and variables for complex logic, you build user interfaces that are predictable, resilient to edge cases, and completely free of stray zeroes or layout flickering.

Where you will meet this

  1. Authentication and Role-Based Navigation: When building application headers, you conditionally render login buttons for guest visitors, user profile avatars for authenticated members, and admin dashboards for staff using ternary operators.
  2. Defensive API Data Consumption: When fetching articles or user profiles from a remote server, you protect components against null or uninitialized data during initial page load using early returns (if (!data) return <SkeletonLoader />;).
  3. Interactive Notification Badges: When displaying notification counters, inbox badges, or shopping cart item totals, you guard numeric values with explicit comparisons (unreadCount > 0 && <Badge />) to eliminate the stray zero bug.

Glossary

  • Conditional Rendering: The ability to show, hide, or switch user interface markup based on JavaScript conditions and props.
  • Early Return: Exiting a component function early with null or fallback markup before executing the main render logic.
  • Ternary Operator: A JavaScript inline conditional expression (? :) that evaluates a condition and returns one of two values.
  • Short-Circuit Evaluation: The evaluation model where logical AND (&&) stops and returns the left operand immediately if it is falsy.
  • Suppression Whitelist: React's built-in rule that renders zero DOM nodes for booleans (true, false), null, and undefined.
  • Stray Zero: An unwanted visible 0 printed on screen when a numeric zero short-circuits on the left side of a logical AND operator.

Beyond the basics

  • Official guide to conditional rendering patterns, if statements, ternaries, and logical AND (see react.dev/learn/conditional-rendering).
  • Official reference documentation explaining how React DOM handles empty nodes, booleans, and null in children (see react.dev/reference/react-dom/components/common).
  • Official guide on preserving and resetting component state across conditional branches (see react.dev/learn/preserving-and-resetting-state).
  • Official documentation on rendering lists and handling empty collections with fallback UI (see react.dev/learn/rendering-lists).

Summary

Architectural Takeaways & Decision Matrix

❒ Operator Selection & Branch Shape

➔ ALWAYS use logical AND (&&) for show-or-nothing branches, and use the ternary operator (? :) when choosing between two alternate elements.

➔ NEVER use two separate inverted && expressions ({isLive && ...}{!isLive && ...}) to simulate an if/else choice.

❒ Numeric Guarding & Falsy Safety

➔ ALWAYS convert numbers to explicit booleans (count > 0 && ...) before using the && operator to prevent the stray zero bug.

➔ NEVER place a raw numeric counter or unverified calculation on the left side of &&.

❒ Complexity Management & DOM Ownership

➔ ALWAYS move complex multi-branch conditions before the return statement using let variables or lookup objects.

➔ NEVER manipulate CSS classes or styles imperatively using classList on DOM elements managed by React.

DO THIS: guard numeric values with explicit boolean comparisons

code.txt
1{commentCount > 0 && (
2 <span className="comments">{commentCount} Comments</span>
3)}

DO NOT DO THIS: pass raw numeric counters to logical AND operators

code.txt
1{commentCount && (
2 <span className="comments">{commentCount} Comments</span>
3)}
