Lecture 11: Rendering Lists and Keys in React

Interview Question

CORE

How do you render a list from an array, and why does React demand a key on every item?

Imagine this scenario:

  1. Marcus sits down at his workstation at The National Times to build the morning news feed.
  2. The editorial team provides a list of breaking stories as a JavaScript array, and Marcus needs to display each story as an interactive card on the homepage.
  3. When an urgent breaking headline arrives at the top of the feed, Marcus prepends it to the array, but an editor's typed correction note on the first story suddenly jumps to the new breaking headline.
  4. Why does React attach existing user input to the wrong story when a new item is added to the front of a list?
  5. Relying on array indices as keys or omitting keys entirely causes React to match elements by position rather than identity, scrambling form inputs, audio players, and checkboxes across unrelated items.
  6. Many developers also struggle with blank screens when their array map callback uses curly braces but forgets the explicit return statement.
  7. Today, we master transforming data arrays into JSX elements using the map method, understand how keys provide persistent identity across renders, and build resilient list interfaces.

The Friction of Static Repetition and Dynamic Feeds

Every modern web application displays dynamic collections of data (such as articles in a news feed, products in a catalog, or messages in an inbox). In basic HTML, every item is written by hand as a separate tag. When you build applications with React, writing hardcoded tags for every item (<StoryCard story={story1} /> <StoryCard story={story2} />) makes code repetitive and rigid. If a newsroom publishes twenty new articles or removes an old report, an engineer would have to edit the component file and redeploy the code.

To see this in action on The National Times, you open your editor to build the main news feed: src/App.jsx. The editorial team gives you an array of story objects from their database. Each story has a unique id, a title, and a category. You want to display these stories in a clean list where editors can type notes directly into each story card.

It is possible that a developer may reach for the array map() method and write {stories.map((story, index) => <StoryRow key={index} story={story} />)} assuming that the array index is a simple and harmless choice for the key. When they do, the initial page appears to render without issues:

Naive Index Key Attempt
1function Feed({ stories }) {
WRONG: Using array index as key causes state drift on prepend
2 return (
3 <ul>
4 {stories.map((story, index) => (
5 <li key={index}><input placeholder="Add note..." /></li>
6 ))}
7 </ul>
8 );
9}

Notice what happens when the collection changes. Suppose an editor types "verify budget figures" into the note input for the first story ("City Transit Accord Finalized"). Suddenly, breaking news occurs, and an urgent story is prepended to the top of the array at index 0. The browser updates, but the editor's typed note does not stay with the transit story. Instead, the note "verify budget figures" now appears inside the note input for the brand new urgent story!

This bug happens because index keys force React to match elements by their numerical position (0 to 0, 1 to 1) rather than their real identity. When the new story enters at index 0, React compares the previous index 0 with the new index 0. React updates the text title inside the existing DOM node, but it leaves the internal input text untouched. The physical input stays at index 0, attached to the wrong article.

To solve this problem, React combines standard JavaScript array transformations with stable element keys. Instead of hardcoding markup or using fragile indices, you transform arrays of data into arrays of JSX elements using .map(). Crucially, you assign each item a stable, unique key prop based on permanent data (such as a database ID). This key gives each item a permanent identity across renders, ensuring that React moves the physical DOM node and its typed text to the correct new position.

⚡ IN THE WILD

Why do user inputs jump to the wrong item when using index keys?

When using array indices as keys (key={index}), React tracks elements purely by their numerical order rather than their data identity. When an item is prepended at index 0, every existing item shifts down by one position. React looks at index 0, sees that the title text changed, and mutates the existing DOM node in place. However, the browser's internal input buffer lives directly inside the physical DOM node. Because React reuses the existing node at index 0 instead of moving it, whatever text the user typed stays in that first box. To the user, their typed input appears to jump to the wrong story. To prevent this, you must always provide a permanent database ID (key={story.id}) so React can move the actual DOM node to its new position.

How JavaScript Transforms Arrays and How React Understands Collections

To understand how React renders lists, we must first look at what a list actually is in React. React does not introduce a proprietary <List> component or a custom loop directive like v-for or *ngFor. In React, a list is simply a standard JavaScript array containing JSX elements. In earlier lessons, you learned that curly braces {} inside JSX open an evaluation window for JavaScript expressions. When you put an array of JSX elements inside curly braces—such as {[<li key="1">A</li>, <li key="2">B</li>]}—React unpacks that array and renders each item in sequential order into the browser DOM.

For developers who are newer to JavaScript, let us briefly review the map() array method. The map() method is a standard JavaScript function available on all arrays. It takes a callback function, runs that function once on each item in the array, and returns a brand-new array containing the transformed items. The original array remains completely untouched. For example, [1, 2, 3].map(n => n * 2) produces [2, 4, 6]. In React, instead of multiplying numbers, our callback function takes a data object (like a story) and returns a JSX element (like <StoryRow key={story.id} story={story} />).

Next, let us review the difference between an arrow function with an implicit return and an arrow function with a block body. In JavaScript, when you write an arrow function without curly braces on the right side of the arrow (story => <StoryRow story={story} />), JavaScript uses an implicit return. It automatically returns the expression right after the arrow. However, if you add curly braces after the arrow (story => { ... }), you create a block body. A block body executes code statements line by line, but it returns undefined unless you explicitly write the return keyword. If you write stories.map(story => { <StoryRow story={story} /> }) the callback returns undefined for every story, and your list renders completely blank.

Finally, we must understand why React demands a key prop on every item in a list. When an application updates, React creates a new tree of element descriptions and compares it with the previous tree to decide what needs to change in the browser DOM. When React compares two lists of child elements, it needs a way to tell which item in the new list matches which item in the old list. Without keys, React falls back to positional matching: it compares the first new item to the first old item, the second to the second, and so on. If an item is inserted, deleted, or reordered, positional matching overwrites DOM nodes in place and scrambles state. With unique, stable keys, React can track each item throughout its lifetime, moving existing DOM nodes smoothly and preserving user inputs.

Principles of React: The Core Laws of Lists and Keys

When preparing for technical interviews, candidates must clearly explain how to transform arrays into JSX, why block bodies in arrow functions can cause silent blank screens, how React uses keys during reconciliation, why array indices and random numbers make dangerous keys, and why child components cannot read props.key. To master these concepts, we formalize the six governing principles of lists and keys:

PRINCIPLE 1

Build a List by Mapping Data to an Array of Elements

array transformation converting an array of raw data objects into a new array of JSX element descriptors using map
declarative list rendering placing an array of element descriptors inside JSX curly braces for React to unpack and render in order

We transform an array of data objects into an array of JSX elements using the standard JavaScript map() method. When we place the resulting array inside JSX curly braces, React automatically renders each element in sequential order. This ensures the structure of the user interface follows the data rather than hardcoded markup.

In React, the user interface is a direct projection of data (UI = f(data)). When you have a collection of items, you do not write imperative loops that append elements to the page one by one. Instead, you call stories.map(story => <StoryRow key={story.id} story={story} />)

Under the hood, map() runs your callback function once for every story in the array and returns a new array of lightweight React element objects in memory.

Data Array to JSX Mapping
1const stories = [
2 { id: 'story-1', title: 'Transit Budget Approved' },
3 { id: 'story-2', title: 'Clean Energy Project Begins' },
4];
5
6const storyElements = stories.map(story => (
7 <li key={story.id}>{story.title}</li>
8));
9console.log(storyElements);
Array of React element objects

When you inspect storyElements in the console, you see an array of plain JavaScript objects, where each object has a type property (such as 'li') and a props property containing { children: story.title }. When you place {storyElements} inside your JSX return statement, React unpacks that array and paints the corresponding DOM elements in sequential order. If the data array grows from two stories to three, React produces three element objects and adds the third node to the screen.

PRINCIPLE 2

Return the JSX from the Map Callback

expression body an arrow function without curly braces that automatically returns the single expression after =>
block body an arrow function with curly braces that requires an explicit return statement to output a value

When writing a map() callback function, ensure it returns a JSX element. If you use an arrow function with curly braces, you must write an explicit return statement. If you omit the return statement, the callback returns undefined for every item, and the list silently renders completely empty.

It is best practice to do this:
stories.map(story => (
<StoryRow key={story.id} story={story} />
Clean implicit return emits element
))
Instead of doing this:
stories.map(story => {
<StoryRow key={story.id} story={story} />
Block body without return yields undefined
})

The official React documentation marks this pattern as an important pitfall because the mistake is completely silent. In JavaScript, an arrow function can be written with an expression body or a block body. In an expression body (story => <StoryRow ... />), there are no curly braces around the body, and JavaScript implicitly returns the value.

However, if you write curly braces after the arrow (story => { <StoryRow ... /> }), JavaScript treats those braces as a code block. Inside a code block, statements execute sequentially, but nothing is returned unless you explicitly write the return keyword.

Implicit vs Explicit Return in Map
1const implicitList = stories.map(story => (
Implicit return: automatically returns element after arrow
2 <StoryRow key={story.id} story={story} />
3));
4
5const explicitList = stories.map(story => {
Explicit return: required when using block body with braces
6 return <StoryRow key={story.id} story={story} />;
7});

When map() runs a block-body callback without a return statement over an array of ten stories, it collects ten undefined values and returns [undefined, undefined, ...]. Because React's suppression whitelist renders zero DOM nodes for undefined, the container element (<ul> or <div>) renders completely blank. The browser console produces no errors and no warnings. Whenever a list renders blank, check whether your arrow function uses curly braces without an explicit return.

PRINCIPLE 3

Put a Unique Key on the Outermost Element Returned by Map

outermost element the top-level JSX tag returned directly by the map callback function
sibling uniqueness the requirement that keys must be distinct among elements within the same array

Place the key prop on the outermost element directly returned inside the map() call, never on elements nested inside a child component. The key must be unique among its sibling elements in that array. If an item returns multiple sibling nodes, wrap them in a <Fragment key={...}> instead of an empty <> tag.

It is best practice to do this:
stories.map(story => (
<StoryRow key={story.id} story={story} />
Key placed on outermost element returned by map
))
Instead of doing this:
stories.map(story => (
<StoryRow story={story} />
Missing key on child component: key placed inside StoryRow root li
))

A frequent mistake happens when developers extract a list row into its own component. When you take the code from <li key={story.id}>{story.title}</li> and move it into a new component named <StoryRow />, you might be tempted to put the key prop on the <li> inside StoryRow.jsx.

When you do this, React immediately prints a warning in the console: "Warning: Each child in a list should have a unique 'key' prop. Check the render method of Feed."

Key on Extracted Row Component
1function Feed({ stories }) {
2 return (
3 <ul>
4 {stories.map(story => (
5 <StoryRow key={story.id} story={story} />
6 ))}
7 </ul>
8 );
9}

React evaluates keys at the array level where the items are mapped. It needs the key directly on the tag returned by the map callback—<StoryRow key={story.id} />—so it knows which <StoryRow> component corresponds to which item. Furthermore, keys only need to be unique among siblings in that specific array; using the same key in a completely different list is completely fine.

Keyed Fragment for Multi-Node Items
1import { Fragment } from 'react';
2
3function StoryList({ stories }) {
4 return stories.map(story => (
5 <Fragment key={story.id}>
6 <dt>{story.title}</dt>
7 <dd>{story.category}</dd>
8 </Fragment>
9 ));
10}

If an item in your list must return two adjacent elements without adding an extra wrapper <div> to the DOM (for example, a <dt> term and a <dd> description in a definition list), you cannot use the empty <>...</> shorthand because shorthand fragments cannot accept props. You must import Fragment from 'react' and write <Fragment key={story.id}>.

PRINCIPLE 4

Treat Keys as the Identity React Uses to Match Items Between Renders

element identity a persistent identifier that ties a virtual element to its physical DOM node across renders
positional diffing React's fallback reconciliation model that compares items by numerical index when keys are missing or unstable

React uses keys as permanent identifiers to match elements between renders. When a list re-renders, React pairs each new element with the previous element that shares the same key and preserves its physical DOM node. Without keys, React pairs elements purely by position, rewriting DOM content in place and breaking local element state.

This principle explains the core mechanism behind React's reconciliation engine. When React renders components into the browser, it creates real DOM nodes. Certain DOM elements hold internal state that lives exclusively inside the browser: text typed into an uncontrolled <input>, the scroll position of a box, or the state of a checkbox.

When a list re-renders, React must decide whether to create new DOM nodes, delete old ones, or update existing nodes.

Array Prepend Mutation Scenario
1const initialFeed = [
2 { id: 'story-1', title: 'City Transit Plan' },
3 { id: 'story-2', title: 'Clean Energy Project' },
4];
5const updatedFeed = [
Urgent story prepended at index 0
6 { id: 'urgent-99', title: 'Flash Flood Alert' },
7 ...initialFeed,
8];

If you do not provide keys, or if you use array indices, React defaults to positional diffing. It compares index 0 to index 0, index 1 to index 1, and so on. When an urgent story is prepended at index 0, the story that was previously at index 0 moves to index 1. Because React compares by position, it looks at index 0, sees that the title changed, and updates the text of the existing DOM node in place. However, the browser's internal input buffer is not touched; whatever the user typed into the input at index 0 stays in that physical DOM node. To the user, their typed note suddenly jumps to the new urgent story!

When you provide stable keys (key={story.id}), React matches the previous story-1 element with the new story-1 element. It sees that story-1 moved from index 0 to index 1, and it physically moves the existing DOM node in the page. The input text, focus, and cursor position move along with their story.

PRINCIPLE 5

Key Items by a Stable ID from the Data, Never by Array Index or Random Values

stable identifier a permanent ID tied to a data entity that never changes throughout the application lifetime
random key churn generating keys on the fly during render, causing React to destroy and recreate the entire DOM tree on every update

Always use a permanent, stable identifier from your data as the key, such as a database ID or a unique ID created when the item was first generated. Never use the array index for lists that can change, and never generate keys during render using Math.random(). Random keys force React to recreate all DOM nodes on every render, losing focus and destroying performance.

It is best practice to do this:
stories.map(story => (
<StoryRow key={story.id} story={story} />
Stable database ID persists across renders
))
Instead of doing this:
stories.map(story => (
<StoryRow key={Math.random()} story={story} />
Random key forces complete DOM teardown and recreation on every render
))

A key must be stable across renders. There are three common sources of keys: permanent database IDs from server data (story.id), locally generated IDs created once when an item is created (crypto.randomUUID()), and array indices.

You should only use the array index as a key if your list meets three strict conditions: the list is completely static, it will never be filtered or reordered, and items will never be added or removed.

Stable Data ID vs Random Key Churn
1stories.map(story => (
BEST PRACTICE: Permanent entity ID created at data inception
2 <StoryRow key={story.id} story={story} />
3));
4
5stories.map(story => (
WRONG: Random key on each render destroys and recreates DOM
6 <StoryRow key={Math.random()} story={story} />
7));

Generating keys on the fly during render with key={Math.random()} is even worse than using indices. Because Math.random() executes on every single render pass, every element gets a completely new key every time the component updates.

When React compares the new tree with the old tree, none of the keys match. React assumes that all previous items were deleted and that completely new items were created. It tears down all existing DOM nodes and rebuilds them from scratch. This drops typing focus, wipes input values, and causes noticeable visual lag. Keys must remain constant across renders for the same data entity.

PRINCIPLE 6

Pass the ID as Its Own Prop When the Component Needs It

reserved prop a prop like key or ref that React consumes internally and excludes from props
explicit data passing passing an identifier under a distinct prop name so child components can read it

React reserves the key prop for its internal reconciliation engine and does not pass it down to your component. If a child component needs the story's ID for links, event handlers, or accessibility labels, you must pass it as a separate, explicitly named prop such as id={story.id} or pass the entire story object.

It is best practice to do this:
<StoryRow key={story.id} id={story.id} story={story} />
Explicit id prop accessible inside child component
Instead of doing this:
<StoryRow key={story.id} story={story} />
Component attempts to read props.key directly, yielding undefined

Developers are often surprised to find that reading props.key inside a child component returns undefined. If an engineer writes <button onClick={() => deleteStory(props.key)}>Delete</button> the delete function receives undefined, and React prints a warning in the console: "Warning: StoryRow: key is not a prop. Trying to access it will result in undefined being returned. If you need to access the same value within the child component, you should pass it as a different prop."

Passing Entity IDs as Dedicated Props
1function Feed({ stories }) {
Parent passes key for React and storyId for component logic
2 return stories.map(story => (
3 <StoryRow key={story.id} storyId={story.id} story={story} />
4 ));
5}
6function StoryRow({ storyId, story }) {
7 return <article data-id={storyId}><h2>{story.title}</h2></article>;
8}

React consumes key (and ref) internally for its fiber and reconciliation system and intentionally strips it from the component's props object. If your component needs the ID—for example, to build a link URL <a href={/story/${storyId}}>, set an HTML data-id attribute, or trigger a callback—you must pass the ID under an ordinary prop name such as id, storyId, or pass the whole story object and read story.id.

Component Summary

App

The root application shell manages the story data collection and maps items into JSX elements. It places the permanent key={story.id} prop on each row component, ensuring React can identify and match items across renders.

StoryRowstory={story}

The list item boundary encapsulates the presentation of a single story. It mounts the category badge, displays the headline, and provides an editor input field whose DOM state is preserved by React's key matching.

CategoryBadgecategory={...}

The leaf category badge formats and styles the category name into a colored pill. It acts as a pure presentation leaf with zero awareness of list mapping or parent keys.

Rendering lists in React is built on standard JavaScript array transformations and explicit element identity. By using map() to project data arrays into JSX descriptors, your application's user interface stays perfectly synchronized with your data. By placing stable, unique keys on the outermost element returned by map(), you give React the identity information it needs to preserve DOM nodes, protect user inputs, and update lists efficiently.

Where you will meet this

  1. Dynamic Content Feeds and Catalogs: In news portals, social media feeds, and product catalogs, you map collections of server data into card components, using permanent entity database IDs as keys to allow smooth filtering and insertion.
  2. Interactive Form Repeaters: In invoice generators, survey builders, or recipe ingredient lists where users can add, remove, and reorder input rows, stable keys ensure that typed text and active cursor focus never jump between rows when an item is deleted.
  3. Tabbed Navigation and Menus: When rendering navigation bars or tab lists from an array of routes, stable keys allow React to track which tab is active without tearing down DOM nodes during tab switching.

Glossary

  • Array Transformation ◼ Using methods like map to convert an array of raw data objects into a new array of JSX element descriptors.
  • Key Prop ◼ A special string or number attribute passed to list elements that React uses to identify items across renders.
  • Positional Diffing ◼ React's fallback reconciliation behavior when keys are absent or based on array index, comparing elements purely by sequential position.
  • Element Identity ◼ The association between a React virtual element and its persistent browser DOM node established by a stable key.
  • Key Churn ◼ An antipattern where keys change on every render (such as from Math.random), forcing React to destroy and recreate all DOM nodes.
  • Reserved Prop ◼ A prop such as key or ref that React consumes internally for reconciliation and does not pass down to the component.

Beyond the basics

  • Official guide on rendering data from arrays and keeping list items in order with keys (see react.dev/learn/rendering-lists).
  • Official reference documentation explaining why keys are required on list children in createElement (see react.dev/reference/react/createElement).
  • Official reference documentation on rendering a list of Fragments with keys (see react.dev/reference/react/Fragment).
  • Official deep dive on preserving and resetting component state using keys across renders (see react.dev/learn/preserving-and-resetting-state).

Summary

Architectural Takeaways & Decision Matrix

❒ Array Transformation & Return Syntax

➔ ALWAYS use array.map() to project data arrays into JSX element arrays inside curly braces.

➔ NEVER forget to write an explicit return statement when using a block body (=> { ... }) in a map callback, which causes the list to render blank.

❒ Key Placement & Multi-Node Grouping

➔ ALWAYS place the key prop on the outermost element directly returned by the map() callback.

➔ NEVER use empty shorthand <>...</> tags inside a mapped list when an item renders multiple siblings; always use <Fragment key={item.id}>.

❒ Key Source & Reconciliation Safety

➔ ALWAYS use permanent, stable entity IDs from your data (such as database IDs) as list keys.

3))}

Lecture 12: Keeping Components Pure

Interview Question

CORE

What does it mean for a component to be pure, and what breaks when it is not?

Imagine this scenario:

  1. Leo sits at his desk at The National Times to build the morning reading list.
  2. The editorial team wants each story to display its position number and an urgent status badge.
  3. Leo creates an outside counter variable and increments it inside the component body, but the numbers jump to two and four on initial page load.
  4. Why does React double the counter numbers even though the page loaded only once?
  5. Writing to variables outside the component or mutating DOM nodes during render corrupts application data and triggers silent layout crashes.
  6. Many developers assume React has a bug when console logs fire twice, unaware that StrictMode deliberately runs components twice to catch side effects.
  7. Today, we master the laws of pure rendering, discover how local mutation works, and build resilient components that calculate markup predictably.

The Friction of Impure Rendering and Shared Variables

Every web application exists to present dynamic data (such as articles, user profiles, or shopping carts) in a clear visual layout. In standard JavaScript, developers often declare shared variables and write step-by-step scripts that alter the page as events occur. React takes a completely different approach: it treats every component as a self-contained calculation that converts inputs directly into user interface descriptors.

To see this in action on The National Times, you open your editor to build the morning reading list: src/App.jsx. You have a collection of news articles, and you want each card to display its sequence number, such as Article #1, Article #2, and Article #3.

It is possible that a developer may declare a counter variable outside the component and increment it inside the function body: let articleCount = 0; function Article() { articleCount = articleCount + 1; ... } When they test this in a basic script, it seems to work. But when they open their browser with a modern React development setup, they immediately notice a bizarre bug: the first article displays #2, the second displays #4, and the third displays #6!

Naive Counter Attempt
1let articleCount = 0;
External module variable
2function Article({ title }) {
3 articleCount = articleCount + 1;
WRONG: mutates outside variable
4 return (
5 <article className="card">
6 <h3>#{articleCount}: {title}</h3>
7 </article>
8 );
9}

Why did the numbers double? In development mode, React wraps your application tree in <StrictMode>. StrictMode deliberately runs every component function twice on each render. Because articleCount lives outside the component, the first call increments it to 1, and the second call increments it to 2. The browser displays the result of the second call. If the user clicks a button or types into an input that triggers a re-render, the counter never resets; it keeps climbing to #8, #10, and #12.

To fix this bug, React requires you to treat your components as pure functions. Instead of mutating an outside counter, the parent component calculates the item number directly from the array index and passes it downward as an explicit prop: <Article itemNumber={index + 1} title={title} /> Because the child component reads only its props, React can run it any number of times without corrupting data.

⚡ IN THE WILD

Why does my component log twice on page load?

In modern React applications, the starter template wraps your root component in <StrictMode>. In development mode, <StrictMode> deliberately invokes every component function twice during every render pass. If you place console.log('render') at the top level of your component body, you will see two messages in the browser console for a single page load. Many developers assume their setup has an infinite loop or a duplicate mount bug, and some even delete <StrictMode> from main.jsx to silence the logs. Do not remove StrictMode! React double-renders your components as an intentional stress test to catch accidental side effects, such as mutating global variables or modifying DOM nodes during render. If your component is a pure function, running it twice produces identical markup and causes zero problems on screen. If running your component twice changes what the user sees, StrictMode has successfully warned you about an impure calculation before your users encounter it in production.

Components as Mathematical Formulas and the Render Contract

To write reliable React applications, we must understand what functional purity means in programming. In mathematics, a formula like y = 2x is pure. If x is 2, y is always 4. If x is 3, y is always 6. The answer does not depend on what time of day it is, what other equations were solved earlier, or how many times you calculate the formula. A pure function obeys two simple laws:

  1. It minds its own business: it does not change any variable, object, or system that existed before it was called.
  2. Same inputs, same output: given the same arguments, it will always return the exact same result.

React builds on this mathematical model: UI = f(props). A component takes props as inputs and calculates a tree of JSX element descriptors as its output. When you keep components pure, React can run them whenever it needs to: it can call them twice in development, render siblings in any order, or discard a render in memory without committing changes to the browser DOM.

Every line of code at the top level of your component function body runs during the render phase. During this phase, React is only calculating what the screen should look like. Because this calculation can run multiple times, the render phase must remain completely free of side effects. A side effect is any action that modifies the outside world, such as changing document.title, writing to the DOM with document.getElementById(), starting a timer, or sending an analytics report. Side effects do not belong in the render body; they belong inside event handlers (such as button clicks) that run outside of render when a user interacts with the page.

Developers often wonder: does purity mean I can never mutate anything in JavaScript? No! React allows local mutation. Local mutation means changing variables, objects, or arrays that you created inside that exact same render call. For example, if you create a local array const items = []; inside your function and push JSX elements into it using a loop, that code is 100% pure. Because the array was born inside that function call, no code outside the component can observe the mutation. However, modifying a variable defined outside the function, mutating a prop, or mutating an array after it has been passed to JSX is forbidden because other components can see those changes.

Let us review three common JavaScript tools used in pure components. First, object destructuring (function Article({ title, minutes })) unpacks properties directly from the props object into local variables. Second, the array spread operator ([...articles, newArticle]) creates a brand-new array containing all previous items plus the new item, leaving the original array completely untouched. Third, the ternary conditional operator (condition ? valueIfTrue : valueIfFalse) is JavaScript's inline if-else shortcut. If the condition before the question mark is true, it evaluates the expression before the colon; otherwise, it evaluates the expression after. Because a ternary operator resolves to a value, it can sit safely inside JSX curly braces to calculate dynamic text and CSS classes purely during render.

Principles of React: The Core Laws of Pure Rendering

When preparing for senior technical interviews, candidates must clearly articulate what makes a component pure, why development double-rendering exists, how local mutation differs from external mutation, why direct DOM writes fail during render, and why non-idempotent functions break the render contract. To master these concepts, we formalize the four governing laws of pure rendering:

PRINCIPLE 1

Treat a Component as a Formula React May Run Any Number of Times

pure component a component function that produces identical JSX for identical inputs and causes zero outside side effects
StrictMode double-rendering a development-only check where React calls component functions twice to detect unexpected side effects

A pure component returns the same JSX for the same props and changes nothing outside itself. React decides when and how often to call your component function: twice per render under StrictMode in development, again whenever its inputs change, and in no guaranteed order between siblings.

In React, component execution is an on-demand calculation. React does not sign a contract promising to run your component function exactly once per screen update. Under <StrictMode> in development, React intentionally renders your component twice.

If you place console.log('render Article:', itemNumber) inside the component body, you will see two log lines in the browser console on a single page load. If you use React DevTools, the second log line appears slightly dimmed to indicate that it came from the development check. In a production build, the check is completely stripped, and the component renders once.

StrictMode Double Call Verification
1export default function Article({ title, itemNumber }) {
2 console.log('render Article:', itemNumber);
Double-invoked by StrictMode
3 return (
4 <article className="card">
5 <h3>#{itemNumber}: {title}</h3>
6 </article>
7 );
8}

If your component is a pure formula, calling it once, twice, or ten times produces the exact same JSX tree and changes nothing in memory. What breaks when developers forget this model is that they treat the double call as a bug, remove StrictMode, and leave hidden mutation bugs that explode later in production.

PRINCIPLE 2

Change Nothing That Existed Before the Render

external mutation changing a variable, array, or object that existed before the current component render call
local mutation modifying a fresh variable or array created inside the current render call before passing it to JSX

During render, never write to variables declared outside the component or mutate objects received as props. You may create fresh arrays or objects inside the function body and mutate them locally, provided that mutation finishes before the value is passed to JSX.

It is best practice to do this:
function ArticleList({ stories }) {
const list = [...stories, { id: 'ad' }];
Fresh local array
return <Feed stories={list} />;
}
Instead of doing this:
function ArticleList({ stories }) {
stories.push({ id: 'ad' });
Mutating props in place
return <Feed stories={stories} />;
}

When a component runs, anything created before that function call is off-limits for mutation. This includes variables declared at the module level, global window properties, and objects or arrays passed in as props.

If you call stories.push(...) on an array received as a prop, you mutate the caller's memory. Under StrictMode, that push() executes twice, resulting in two identical ad items in the list and triggering React's "Encountered two children with the same key" warning.

Safe Array Copy Pattern
1export default function ArticleList({ articles, featured }) {
2 const fullList = [...articles, featured];
Creates fresh local array
3 return (
4 <section className="feed">
5 {fullList.map((story) => (
6 <p key={story.id}>{story.title}</p>
7 ))}
8 </section>
9 );
10}

Similarly, if you mutate a local object after passing it into a JSX element—such as setting styles.color = 'red' after writing <Header styles={styles} />—the earlier element receives the modified value because both share the same object reference in memory. In contrast, creating a new array inside the function and mutating it is completely safe: const cards = []; for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) cards.push(<Card key={i} />); Because cards was created in that render call, no other component can see it.

PRINCIPLE 3

Keep Side Effects Out of the Render Path

side effect any operation that modifies state outside the current function or interacts with outside systems
render path the synchronous code executed at the top level of a component function to calculate markup

The component body exists strictly to calculate JSX. Never modify DOM nodes, start timers, send network requests, or trigger analytics from the top level of your component function. Express dynamic visual changes in the returned JSX, and move side effects into event handlers.

It is best practice to do this:
function Badge({ isUrgent }) {
const cls = isUrgent ? 'urgent' : 'normal';
Pure JSX class
return <span className={cls}>News</span>;
}
Instead of doing this:
function Badge({ isUrgent }) {
const badge = document.getElementById('badge');
badge.className = 'urgent';
Mutating DOM directly
return <span id="badge">News</span>;
}

A frequent pitfall for developers transitioning to React is trying to change the page imperatively during render. For example, if you write document.getElementById('badge').className = 'urgent' directly in the component body, the code fails with a fatal error on the initial render: TypeError: Cannot set properties of null (setting 'className')

The error occurs because the component function runs before React creates or mounts the browser DOM elements. The element #badge does not exist in the document yet. Even if the element already existed from an earlier render, modifying DOM properties by hand bypasses React's reconciliation engine and creates desynchronized interfaces.

Declarative Class Computation
1export default function StatusBadge({ isUrgent, label }) {
2 const badgeClass = isUrgent
3 ? 'badge-urgent'
Urgent status styling
4 : 'badge-standard';
5 return (
6 <span className={badgeClass}>
7 {label}
8 </span>
9 );
10}

The pure React solution is to express the desired class directly in the returned markup using a ternary operator: <span className={isUrgent ? 'urgent' : 'normal'}> When you need to perform real side effects—such as sending an HTTP request or updating analytics—place that code inside an event handler (which runs on user interaction) rather than in the render path.

PRINCIPLE 4

Avoid Non-Idempotent Calls in Render Output

non-idempotent function a function that produces a different return value each time it is invoked, even with identical arguments
idempotent rendering running a component with the same inputs always produces the exact same JSX output

Calling non-idempotent functions like Math.random() or new Date() directly in the component body produces different values on every call, breaking the guarantee that identical inputs yield identical JSX. Pass dynamic numbers and timestamps in as props from outside the render.

It is best practice to do this:
function TimeDisplay({ publishedAt }) {
return <span>{publishedAt}</span>;
Deterministic prop
}
Instead of doing this:
function TimeDisplay() {
const now = new Date().toISOString();
Impure clock call
return <span>{now}</span>;
}

A function is idempotent if executing it multiple times with the same inputs produces the exact same result. When you write const id = Math.random() or const time = new Date() inside your component body, you introduce non-idempotent code into the render path.

Under StrictMode in development, the first call generates one random number (such as 0.791), and the second call generates a completely different number (such as 0.029). The browser console displays two disagreeing values, and the screen displays whichever happened to run last.

Idempotent Prop Timestamp
1export default function ArticleTime({ timestamp }) {
2 return (
3 <time className="published-date">
4 {timestamp}
Prop timestamp passed downward from parent
5 </time>
6 );
7}

Furthermore, calling new Date() in the render body freezes the time at the exact millisecond the component rendered, meaning the clock never ticks forward unless something triggers a re-render. To preserve purity, generate random identifiers or capture the current timestamp outside of the component render—such as passing it downward as a prop from an event handler or data store.

In src/components/ArticleCard.jsx we construct the presentation card. The component receives itemNumber, title, and minutes through object destructuring.

Notice what is absent from this file: there are zero calls to document.getElementById(), zero increments of module variables, and zero array mutations. The card acts as a pure calculation: given the same inputs, it produces the exact same article markup and nests the child badge component cleanly.

ArticleCard.jsx

By keeping ArticleCard pure, it has no hidden dependencies on sibling cards or external state. It receives everything it needs to display through props and delegates the reading duration to StatusBadge.

In src/components/StatusBadge.jsx we build the terminal status badge. The component receives the reading duration in minutes. If the article takes longer than six minutes, it is labeled "In-Depth Read"; otherwise, it is labeled "Quick Read".

Notice how the CSS class and label text are determined: we use JavaScript ternary conditional operators directly inside the function. We never query the browser DOM or alter class lists imperatively. React evaluates the ternary expression during render and updates the browser node atomically.

Component Summary

App

The reading desk shell defines the article collection and calculates itemNumber purely from the array mapping index without outside mutable variables.

ArticleCarditemNumber={1}

The pure article card receives data through props and renders structured markup with zero DOM queries or external mutations.

StatusBadgeminutes={4}

The pure status badge evaluates ternary operators directly in the JSX return to compute dynamic class names atomically.

Look at how this three-file architecture fulfills the pure rendering contract. In a naive implementation, an engineer might have created a mutable counter in App.jsx, pushed badges into an outside array in ArticleCard.jsx, and queried document.getElementById() in StatusBadge.jsx. Under StrictMode, that naive setup would display doubled counts (#2, #4), crash with null selector exceptions on initial load, and leak state across renders.

By treating every component as a pure mathematical formula, data flows downward cleanly through props. React can invoke any component in this tree any number of times, and the browser will always render the exact same user interface.

Where you will meet this

  1. Server-Side Rendering and Static Site Generation: Because pure components produce identical markup for identical inputs, server frameworks like Next.js can safely run your component tree on a server to generate HTML for thousands of concurrent reader requests without cross-request state contamination.
  2. Performance Caching with Memoization: When a component is pure, React can safely skip re-rendering it if its props have not changed (React.memo), caching the previous output because a pure formula is guaranteed to return the exact same JSX.
  3. Interrupted Concurrent Rendering: When React prioritizes urgent user inputs over background updates, it can pause or abort a component render halfway through and restart it later; pure components guarantee that aborted renders leave zero corrupted traces behind.
  4. Automated Unit Testing: Testing pure components is straightforward and reliable because you do not need to mock global document properties, reset external counter variables, or clean up leaked side effects between test cases.

Glossary

  • Pure Function: A function that always returns the exact same result given the same inputs and produces zero side effects on preexisting variables or outside systems.
  • Side Effect: Any operation that modifies state outside the current function or interacts with outside systems (such as DOM mutations, timers, network requests, or analytics) during execution.
  • StrictMode: A React development-only wrapper component that deliberately executes component functions twice to expose unintended side effects and impure rendering logic.
  • Local Mutation: Modifying variables, arrays, or objects created within the current render execution before they are passed into JSX, which remains 100% pure.
  • Idempotence: The property of a code block or function where executing it multiple times with identical inputs produces the exact same outcome without state drift.

Beyond the basics

  • Understanding the mathematical foundation of pure components and how React treats UI calculations as declarative formulas (see react.dev/learn/keeping-components-pure).
  • Comprehensive reference rules on why components and hooks must be pure and how React schedules render and commit phases (see react.dev/reference/rules/components-and-hooks-must-be-pure).
  • Enabling and understanding StrictMode development checks, double-rendering mechanics, and log dimming in browser developer tools (see react.dev/reference/react/StrictMode).
  • How pure components enable advanced performance optimizations and skip redundant renders when inputs remain identical (see react.dev/reference/react/memo).
  • The architectural rules governing when and where side effects belong inside event handlers or synchronization mechanisms (see react.dev/learn/responding-to-events).

Summary

Architectural Takeaways & Decision Matrix

❒ Pure Render Calculations

➔ ALWAYS treat your component function as a pure mathematical formula: UI = f(props).

➔ ALWAYS pass dynamic values like item numbers, timestamps, and counters downward as explicit props rather than incrementing external variables.

DO THIS: derive numbering directly from array mapping or props

2 return (

5 <Article key={story.id} itemNumber={i + 1} title={story.title} />
6 ))}
7 </div>
8 );
9}

DO NOT DO THIS: increment outside variables inside the render body

1let count = 0;
2function Article({ title }) {
3 count = count + 1;
4 return <h3>#{count}: {title}</h3>;
5}
❒ Managing Mutation and Data Flow

➔ NEVER mutate variables, arrays, or objects that existed before the component was called.

➔ IF you need to accumulate or format items during render THEN use local mutation on fresh arrays created within the same function call.

➔ NEVER mutate a local object after it has been passed into a JSX element.

DO THIS: copy arrays with spread syntax to avoid mutating props

code.txt
1function StoryTray({ stories, bonusStory }) {
2 const allStories = [...stories, bonusStory];

4}

4}
❒ Side Effects and Browser Interaction

➔ NEVER write to DOM nodes, start timers, or trigger network analytics directly inside the component body.

➔ IF you need visual class changes based on data THEN calculate them declaratively in JSX using ternary conditional operators.

➔ ALWAYS place interactive side effects inside event handlers that run outside of the render phase.

Lecture 13: Responding to Events and Callback Props

Interview Question

CORE

How do you respond to user events like clicks and typing, and how do callback props communicate back to parents?

Imagine this scenario:

  1. Leo opens his code editor at The National Times to add interactive buttons to the morning reading desk.
  2. The editorial team wants readers to select stories for reading and save articles for later.
  3. Leo writes onClick={handleSelect(article.id)}, but the function fires instantly for every article during page load and does nothing when clicked.
  4. Why does adding parentheses after a handler cause it to run during render instead of waiting for a user click?
  5. Invoking handlers during render triggers premature actions, while custom components silently ignore unwired event props.
  6. Many developers struggle with passing function references versus calling functions, and build inaccessible click targets with plain div tags.
  7. Today, we master passing event handlers, learn how callback props communicate upward to parents, and build accessible button controls.

The Friction of Premature Execution and Custom Props

Every web application exists to present dynamic content, but real user interfaces must also respond when users interact with the screen. Users click buttons, submit search queries, and save articles for later reading. In earlier lessons, you learned that React components are pure functions that calculate JSX markup from incoming props. However, when developers begin adding interactivity to their components, they frequently carry habits from traditional scripting that clash with React's declarative rendering model.

To see this in action on The National Times, Leo sits at his desk to build the interactive reading desk: src/App.jsx. He renders a list of news articles and wants each card to feature a "Read Article" button. When the reader clicks the button, the application should log the selected article ID to the console.

It is common for an engineer to write onClick={openArticle(id)} on the button, expecting React to store the function and its argument until the user clicks. But when they open their browser, they immediately see an alarming failure: the console prints "Opened article: art-1" and "Opened article: art-2" immediately on page load, before the user touches anything! Even worse, when the user clicks the button later, nothing happens at all.

Naive Execution Attempt
1function ArticleCard({ title, id }) {
2 function openArticle(articleId) {
3 console.log('Opened article:', articleId);
4 }
5 return (
6 <button onClick={openArticle(id)}>
Evaluates immediately on page load during render
7 Read {title}
8 </button>
9 );
10}

Why did the function execute on page load? In JSX, any expression placed inside curly braces evaluates immediately during the render phase. When JavaScript encounters openArticle(id), it executes the function right then and there. Because openArticle does not return another function, it returns undefined. React assigns undefined to the onClick prop, leaving the button with no click handler when the user finally interacts with the page.

A second common failure occurs when an engineer passes an event prop to a custom component, such as writing <ArticleCard onClick={handleSelect} /> Custom components are JavaScript functions, not browser DOM elements. React does not attach browser event listeners to custom component tags. If ArticleCard does not explicitly receive that prop and pass it down to a native browser element like <button>, the event prop is completely ignored and clicks are silently lost.

⚡ IN THE WILD

Why did my button click handler run on page load?

In JSX, expressions inside curly braces run immediately during component rendering. If you write onClick={openArticle(story.id)} JavaScript executes openArticle right away while constructing the element tree. The function runs on page load before the user touches anything, and its return value (undefined) is passed to onClick, leaving the button unresponsive when clicked later. To fix this, wrap the call in an arrow function: onClick={() => openArticle(story.id)} The arrow function acts as a delayed container: it is created during render, but its inner code executes only when the user triggers the click event.

Event Handlers as Functions and the DOM Boundary

To build predictable user interfaces in React, we must understand how React connects JavaScript functions to browser events. In the browser DOM, elements dispatch events (such as click, input, keydown, and submit) when users interact with the screen. In standard HTML, developers used lowercase attributes like onclick="handleClick()". In React, event props are written in camelCase, such as onClick, onChange, onKeyDown, and onSubmit. Instead of passing a string containing code, you pass an actual JavaScript function value. When the user interacts with the rendered element, React receives the native browser event and invokes your handler function.

A fundamental rule of React is the distinction between passing a function reference and calling a function. When you write onClick={handleClick}, you are giving React the address of the function; you are saying, "Remember this function and execute it when the user clicks this button." But when you write onClick={handleClick()}, the parentheses tell JavaScript to execute handleClick right now, while the component function is running. The return value of handleClick is then assigned to onClick. If you need to pass an argument to a handler, you must not call it directly in JSX. Instead, you create a new function on the fly using an arrow function: onClick={() => handleSelect(article.id)} Because the arrow function body does not execute until the arrow function itself is called, the inner handleSelect call waits safely until the user clicks.

A frequent source of confusion is understanding where browser events stop and React component props begin. Built-in HTML elements (like <button>, <input>, <a>, and <form>) represent real browser DOM elements; React attaches native event listeners to these built-in elements. In contrast, custom components (like <ArticleCard /> or <BookmarkButton />) are purely JavaScript abstractions. If you write <ArticleCard onClick={handleClick} /> React does not attach a click listener to any DOM node because ArticleCard is not a DOM node. The prop onClick is merely a custom prop, exactly like title or color. For that click to do anything, ArticleCard must receive the prop and attach it to a real built-in element inside its return markup: <button onClick={onClick}>. By convention, custom components name their handler props after the application action (such as onSelect or onBookmark) rather than low-level DOM events. The parent decides what action should occur, passes a callback function down, and the child wires that callback to a native button.

Let us review two JavaScript features essential for clean event handling: arrow functions and naming conventions. An arrow function (() => expression) is a concise way to create an anonymous function value in JavaScript. When written as () => onSelect(article.id) it accepts the event and forwards the specific article.id to the parent callback. Second, React developers follow a universal naming convention: handler functions defined inside a component are named with the prefix handle followed by the action or event (such as handleSelect or handleBookmark), while props that receive callbacks are named with the prefix on followed by the action (such as onSelect or onBookmark). This distinction makes code instantly readable: on signals a prop that accepts behavior, while handle signals the function that implements that behavior.

Principles of React: The Core Laws of Event Handling

When preparing for senior technical interviews, candidates must clearly explain why handlers must be passed rather than called, how inline arrow functions pass arguments safely, why custom components require explicit wiring to built-in DOM elements, and why click targets must use semantic button tags. To master these concepts, we formalize the three governing principles of event handling:

PRINCIPLE 1

Pass the Handler, Never Call It

function reference passing the function itself as an uncalled value so an event listener can execute it later
premature invocation executing a function during render by adding parentheses inside JSX braces instead of waiting for user interaction

Give an event prop a function value (onClick={handlePublish}) so React can call it when the user clicks, and when the handler needs arguments, pass a new function that makes the call (onClick={() => openArticle(article.id)}), because anything written inside JSX curly braces runs immediately during render.

We should do this:
<button onClick={handlePublish}>Publish</button>
Passes uncalled function reference to run on click
We should not do this:
<button onClick={handlePublish()}>Publish</button>
Parentheses call the function immediately during render

In React, JSX curly braces are an evaluation window into JavaScript. Any expression placed inside { ... } runs synchronously during the render phase. If you write onClick={handlePublish()}, JavaScript invokes handlePublish() immediately while constructing the JSX element tree. If handlePublish logs "PUBLISH ran" to the console, that message appears on page load before any user interaction. Because handlePublish does not return a function, onClick receives undefined. When the user later clicks the button, the browser finds no function to call, and the click produces zero output.

The exact same defect occurs when passing arguments: writing onClick={openArticle(story.id)} executes openArticle during render for every item in your list. To pass a handler without running it, pass the bare function name: onClick={handlePublish}. When arguments are required, wrap the call inside an arrow function: onClick={() => openArticle(story.id)} The arrow function is an uncalled function value created during render; it runs only when the user dispatches a click event.

Handler Reference vs Immediate Invocation
1export default function PublishButton() {
2 function handlePublish() {
3 console.log('PUBLISH ran');
4 }
5 return (
6 <button type="button" onClick={handlePublish}>
Passes uncalled function reference to run on click
7 Publish Story
8 </button>
9 );
10}

By passing handlePublish without parentheses, React stores the function reference and attaches it to the browser button element. The log "PUBLISH ran" appears strictly when the user clicks the button.

PRINCIPLE 2

Hand Behavior to a Child Through an on Prop and Wire It to a Real Element

callback prop a function prop passed from parent to child allowing the child to report user actions upward
DOM element boundary the terminal built-in HTML elements (like button or input) where React connects event props to browser events

When the parent decides what a click means, pass a function through a prop named for the app action (<ArticleCard onSelect={handleSelect} />) and, inside the child, pass that prop to a built-in element's event prop (<button onClick={() => onSelect(id)}>), because only built-in elements turn browser events into handler calls; a custom component ignores props it does not use.

We should do this:
function ArticleCard({ onSelect, id }) {
Receives custom callback prop from parent
return <button onClick={() => onSelect(id)}>Read</button>;
Wires callback to native button via inline arrow
}
We should not do this:
function ArticleCard({ onSelect }) {
return <div className="card">Read</div>;
Non-interactive div ignores callback prop and drops click events
}

Custom React components are not DOM elements. When you write <ArticleCard onClick={handleClick} /> the browser does not see a DOM element named <ArticleCard>, and React does not attach an event listener to the card boundary. Custom components only receive props; if ArticleCard does not explicitly take onClick and wire it to a built-in element, clicking anywhere on the rendered card does nothing.

To establish clear architectural boundaries, name handler props after the semantic application action rather than generic DOM events: pass onSelect={handleSelect} instead of onClick={handleSelect}. This separation decouples the parent from the child's internal layout: the parent cares that a story was selected, while the child decides whether that selection is triggered by a button, a keypress, or an icon click. Inside the child, connect the callback prop directly to a built-in browser element's event prop: <button onClick={() => onSelect(article.id)}> When the user clicks the button, the child executes the callback, passing relevant identifiers upward while the parent retains full authority over application data.

Parent Callback Delegation
1export default function ArticleCard({ article, onSelect }) {
Callback prop passed down from parent
2 return (
3 <article className="article-card">
4 <h3>{article.title}</h3>
5 <button type="button" onClick={() => onSelect(article.id)}>
Inline arrow function delays execution until user clicks
6 Read Story
7 </button>
8 </article>
9 );
10}

Notice that ArticleCard does not make business decisions about what reading an article means; it simply triggers onSelect(article.id) when the button is clicked, letting the parent handle navigation or data fetching.

PRINCIPLE 3

Make Click Targets Real Buttons

semantic button an HTML button element providing built-in keyboard navigation, focus management, and screen reader accessibility
inaccessible click target a non-interactive element like div or span given an onClick handler without keyboard support

Attach click handlers to <button> elements (or links for navigation), not to <div> or <span>, because the browser gives a button keyboard focus and activation with Enter and Space, while a clickable <div> responds only to a mouse.

We should do this:
<button type="button" className="action-btn" onClick={handleSave}>
Built-in button element with keyboard focus and activation
Save
</button>
We should not do this:
<div className="action-btn" onClick={handleSave}>
Inaccessible click target unreached by Tab or Enter
Save
</div>

A frequent design flaw in modern web applications is turning generic layout containers into clickable controls by writing <div onClick={handleClick}> or <span onClick={handleClick}>. While a mouse click may fire the handler, non-interactive elements lack built-in accessibility. A user navigating with the Tab key cannot move focus to a <div>, and pressing the Enter or Space keys produces zero response. Screen readers announce the element as generic text or a grouping, giving visually impaired users no indication that the element is actionable.

In contrast, the HTML <button> element provides full accessibility out of the box: the browser includes it in the keyboard tab sequence, displays native focus outlines, dispatches click events when the user presses Enter or Space, and communicates its interactive role to assistive technologies. If you need a button to look like a plain link or badge, use CSS to remove the default background and borders (border: none; background: transparent;) while preserving the underlying semantic <button>.

Accessible Button Target
1export default function BookmarkControl({ onSave }) {
2 return (
3 <button type="button" onClick={onSave}>
Passes function reference directly to native button click listener
4 Save to Bookmarks
5 </button>
6 );
7}

Using <button type="button"> guarantees that every user, whether navigating with a mouse, a keyboard, or a screen reader, can interact with your application smoothly.

Component Summary

App

The reading desk shell defines articles and handles user action callbacks without mutating state directly.

ArticleCardonSelect={handleSelect}

The interactive article card wires incoming callback props to child button elements.

BookmarkButtononBookmark={handleBookmark}

The accessible bookmark button renders a native button element that responds to keyboard and mouse clicks.

Examine how this three-file architecture handles user interaction cleanly. In a naive implementation, an engineer might have written onClick={openArticle(id)} directly in App.jsx, causing every article to fire on page load and leaving buttons non-functional. They might have passed onClick to <ArticleCard /> without wiring it internally, leaving clicks ignored. Or they might have created clickable <div onClick> elements that keyboard users cannot reach.

By contrast, our architecture passes uncalled function references downward through on-prefixed props, wraps parameterized calls in inline arrow functions, and connects all user interactions to native <button> elements at the DOM boundary. The child components remain reusable presentation controls, while the parent container retains full decision-making power.

Where you will meet this

  1. Interactive Design Systems and Component Libraries: UI libraries like Material UI or Radix pass callback props like onClick, onSelect, or onValueChange from parent containers down to reusable styled button components.
  2. Form Controls and Input Handlers: Search bars, filters, and text fields accept user input through onChange and onKeyDown, passing user text upward to parent validation and processing handlers.
  3. Modal Dialogs and Drawer Toggles: Overlay dialogs receive onClose callback props from root pages, allowing a child close button to notify the parent when the user requests dismissal.
  4. Accessibility and Keyboard Navigation Audits: Automated accessibility scanners (like axe-core and Lighthouse) check that interactive elements use semantic <button> tags rather than plain <div> elements with click handlers.

Glossary

  • Function Reference: Passing a function by name as an uncalled value without parentheses so React can execute it later when an event fires.
  • Premature Invocation: Accidental execution of a function during the render phase caused by placing parentheses after the function name inside JSX curly braces.
  • Callback Prop: A function passed downward through props from parent to child, allowing the child to report user interactions upward.
  • Inline Arrow Function: An anonymous function expression (() => handler(arg)) created inside JSX to delay function execution until an event occurs while passing arguments.
  • DOM Element Boundary: The terminal built-in HTML elements (such as button, input, or a) where React connects JSX event props directly to browser event listeners.

Beyond the basics

  • Official documentation on common built-in React DOM components and supported event props (see react.dev/reference/react-dom/components/common).
  • Best practices for naming custom event handler props and maintaining component readability (see react.dev/learn/responding-to-events#naming-event-handler-props).
  • Web accessibility standards on semantic buttons versus generic clickable containers (see developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTML/Element/button).
  • Understanding synthetic events, propagation, and preventing default browser actions (see react.dev/learn/responding-to-events#event-propagation).

❒ Event Handler Attachment

➔ ALWAYS pass event handlers as function references without parentheses: onClick={handleClick}.

➔ ALWAYS wrap handlers that require arguments inside an inline arrow function: onClick={() => handleClick(item.id)}

DO THIS: pass function references or arrow functions to event props

❒ Callback Props and Component Boundaries

➔ ALWAYS name callback props after the application action with an on prefix: onSelect={handleSelect}.

➔ ALWAYS wire callback props to built-in DOM elements (like <button>) inside the child component.
